skills.title: Explain that scientific ideas rest on evidence from observation, measurement and experiment, not on authority
Give examples of ideas that changed when new evidence appeared (flat to round Earth, Earth-centred to Sun-centred, Pluto reclassified, heavier objects fall faster)
Test an idea fairly: predict, change one thing at a time, observe, repeat and compare

expectations: Science explains the world using evidence from observations, measurements and experiments, not just someone's opinion or the fame of the person who said it.
When new evidence does not fit an old idea, scientists check it carefully; if it holds up, the idea is changed or replaced.

Example: people once thought the Earth was flat; evidence such as ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon, the round shadow of the Earth on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, and photos from space showed it is round.
Changing an idea because of better evidence is a strength of science, not a failure; ideas are trusted because they keep matching the evidence.
A fair test changes only one thing at a time and repeats the measurement, so the evidence can be trusted.

misconceptions.belief: Scientific knowledge is fixed and never changes once it is in a book.
signs: Says 'it is written in the science book, so it is true forever'
Is shocked or upset that Pluto is no longer called a planet
Cannot name any idea that science has changed

diagnostic.prompt_en: In 2006, scientists decided that Pluto would be called a dwarf planet instead of a planet. What does this show about science?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: 2006 mein scientists ne decide kiya ki Pluto ko planet nahi, dwarf planet kahenge. Isse science ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?

options.text: Science never changes, so this news must be false
New observations of many similar objects made scientists update their definition
Science changed, so science cannot be trusted any more

remediation.representation: A timeline strip of one idea (Earth's shape or Pluto) showing each new piece of evidence as a card added to it
remediation.moveShape: Have the child place evidence cards on the timeline one by one and say after each card whether the old idea still fits

misconceptions.belief: If a scientific idea changes, it means science is just guessing and cannot be trusted.
signs: Says 'scientists keep changing their minds, so why believe them'
Treats an updated idea as proof that all of science is unreliable

diagnostic.prompt_en: Long ago people thought the Sun goes around the Earth. Today we know the Earth goes around the Sun. Which is the best way to see this change?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Bahut pehle log sochte the ki Sun Earth ke chakkar lagata hai. Aaj hum jaante hain ki Earth Sun ke chakkar lagati hai. Is badlav ko kaise samjhein?

options.text: Science corrected itself using better evidence, so today's idea is more reliable
It proves scientists were foolish and science is just guessing
Both ideas are equally right; it depends on what you like

remediation.representation: A 'map that gets better' picture: an old rough map of India next to a modern satellite map
remediation.moveShape: Contrast correcting a map with throwing it away; ask what makes the newer map better

misconceptions.belief: An idea is scientific and true because a famous or important person said it.
signs: Answers 'because a great scientist said so' when asked how we know
Thinks a class vote can settle a science question

diagnostic.prompt_en: The great thinker Aristotle taught that heavier objects fall faster, and people believed it for almost 2000 years. What is the best way to check it?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Mahaan vichaarak Aristotle ne sikhaya ki bhaari cheezein jaldi girti hain, aur log lagbhag 2000 saal tak maante rahe. Ise check karne ka sabse accha tareeka kya hai?

options.text: Believe it, because such a great thinker said it
Drop two balls of different weights from the same height together and watch
Take a vote in class

remediation.representation: A side-by-side: a famous name on one card and a stopwatch-and-ruler on the other, with the label 'which one decides?'
remediation.moveShape: Run a quick drop test after asking for the famous person's claim; let the result, not the name, settle it

misconceptions.belief: Heavier objects always fall faster than lighter ones.
signs: Predicts that a cricket ball will hit the ground well before a tennis ball
Explains falling speed only by weight and never mentions air

diagnostic.prompt_en: A cricket ball and a tennis ball, about the same size, are dropped together from the same height. What will happen?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Cricket ball aur tennis ball, dono lagbhag ek size ki, ek saath ek hi oonchai se giraayi jaati hain. Kya hoga?

options.text: The cricket ball lands much earlier because it is heavier
Both land at almost the same time
The tennis ball lands first because it is lighter

remediation.representation: Slow-motion side-by-side drop video of two balls of different weight but the same size
remediation.moveShape: Predict-observe-explain: get the prediction aloud, drop them, then ask what could make a flat paper fall slower if not weight

items.prompt_en: What is evidence in science? Give one example of evidence you could collect yourself at home.
items.prompt_hi: Science mein 'evidence' kya hota hai? Ek example do jo tum ghar pe khud collect kar sakte ho.
items.answer: Evidence is what we observe or measure that shows whether an idea is right, for example measuring a plant's height every day or timing how long an ice cube takes to melt.
hints: Ask how they would convince a friend who does not believe them
Point to things they can see, count or measure
Prompt: evidence is what we ___ or ___ to check an idea
Assert: evidence is observations and measurements that test an idea

verified.solverAnswer: Evidence is what we observe or measure to test an idea; e.g. measuring a plant's height daily or timing how long ice takes to melt.

items.prompt_en: Name one idea that people believed long ago but changed because of new evidence.
items.prompt_hi: Ek aisa idea batao jo log pehle maante the, par naye evidence ki wajah se badal gaya.
items.answer: For example: the Earth was thought to be flat but is round; the Sun was thought to go around the Earth but the Earth goes around the Sun; Pluto was called a planet but is now a dwarf planet; heavier objects were thought to fall faster but all fall together when air does not get in the way.
hints: Ask what people long ago thought about the shape of the Earth
Point to Pluto or to the Sun and Earth
Prompt: people once thought the Earth was ___, now we know it is ___
Assert: the flat-Earth idea changed to a round Earth because of evidence

verified.solverAnswer: Earth was thought flat/centre of universe; changed to round / Earth goes round Sun after evidence (or Pluto reclassified).

items.prompt_en: Hold a cricket ball and a tennis ball at the same height and let go of both together over grass or a mat. Before you drop them, predict: which will touch the ground first?
items.prompt_hi: Ek cricket ball aur ek tennis ball ko ek hi oonchai pe pakdo aur ghaas ya mat ke upar ek saath chhodo. Chhodne se pehle guess karo: kaun pehle zameen ko chhuegi?
items.answer: They land at almost the same time. When air resistance is small, heavier objects do not fall faster than lighter ones of the same shape.
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason before the drop
Point to the fact that both balls have the same size and shape
Prompt: when air hardly slows them, objects of different weight fall at the ___ rate
Assert: they land together; weight alone does not make things fall faster

verified.solverAnswer: Both land at about the same time (air resistance small); weight alone doesn't decide.

items.prompt_en: Take two identical sheets of paper. Crumple one into a tight ball and keep the other flat. Both weigh exactly the same. Predict: if you drop them together from the same height, which reaches the floor first, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Do bilkul ek jaise kaagaz lo. Ek ko kas ke goli bana do, doosra seedha rehne do. Dono ka wazan bilkul same hai. Guess karo: ek saath giraoge toh kaun pehle zameen pe pahunchega, aur kyon?
items.answer: The crumpled ball lands first. Their weights are equal, so the difference comes from air: the flat sheet pushes against much more air and is slowed down more.
hints: Ask what is different about the two if the weight is the same
Point to how much air each one has to push aside
Prompt: same weight, so the difference must be the ___
Assert: the crumpled ball wins because air slows the flat sheet more

verified.solverAnswer: Crumpled ball lands first; the flat sheet is slowed by more air resistance (larger surface area), same weight.

items.prompt_en: When a ship sails away from the beach, its bottom disappears first and the top of its mast is seen last. Why is this evidence that the Earth is round?
items.prompt_hi: Jab jahaaz beach se door jaata hai, toh pehle uska neeche wala hissa gayab hota hai aur mast ka upar wala hissa sabse aakhir mein dikhta hai. Ye is baat ka evidence kyon hai ki Earth gol hai?
items.answer: On a curved Earth the lower part of the ship goes behind the curve of the surface first. On a flat Earth the whole ship would just get smaller and fade away all at once.
hints: Ask what would happen to the ship's picture if the sea were perfectly flat
Point to the curve of a big ball with an ant walking over it
Prompt: the bottom hides first because it goes behind the ___ of the Earth
Assert: a curved surface hides the bottom first, so the Earth is round

verified.solverAnswer: Curved surface of Earth hides the lower part first behind the curve; on a flat sea the whole ship would shrink evenly.

items.prompt_en: Riya says, 'My dadi says neem leaves keep insects away from stored grain, so it must be true.' Arjun says, 'Let's keep grain in two jars, one with neem leaves and one without, and check both after a month.' Whose way gives scientific evidence, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Riya kehti hai, 'Meri dadi kehti hain neem ke patte rakhe anaaj se keede door rakhte hain, toh ye sach hi hoga.' Arjun kehta hai, 'Do dibbe mein anaaj rakhte hain, ek mein neem ke patte, ek mein nahi, aur ek mahine baad dono dekhte hain.' Kiska tareeka scientific evidence deta hai, aur kyon?
items.answer: Arjun's, because comparing two jars that differ only in the neem leaves tests the idea. Dadi's tip may well be right and is a good idea to test; the fair test turns it into evidence.
hints: Ask which way would convince someone who had never heard dadi's tip
Point to the jar without neem as the one to compare against
Prompt: Arjun changes only ___ thing and compares the two jars
Assert: Arjun's fair test gives evidence; dadi's idea is worth testing

verified.solverAnswer: Arjun's: a fair test with two jars changing only neem gives evidence; Riya's is hearsay/untested (though worth testing).

items.prompt_en: Long ago, most people believed the Sun goes around the Earth. What kind of evidence made scientists change to the idea that the Earth goes around the Sun?
items.prompt_hi: Pehle zyada log maante the ki Sun Earth ke chakkar lagata hai. Kis tarah ke evidence ki wajah se scientists ne maana ki Earth Sun ke chakkar lagati hai?
items.answer: Careful observations and measurements of how planets move in the sky, which fit a Sun-centred picture better; with a telescope Galileo saw moons going around Jupiter and the changing shape of Venus, which did not fit the old idea. Spacecraft confirm it today.
hints: Ask what tool lets us look closely at planets
Point to Galileo seeing small moons circling Jupiter
Prompt: careful ___ of planets through a ___ did not fit the old idea
Assert: observations of planets, especially through telescopes, changed the idea

verified.solverAnswer: Observations through telescopes (Galileo: Jupiter's moons, phases of Venus) and careful planetary positions did not fit the old idea.

items.prompt_en: Your friend says his new water bottle keeps water cold much longer than your steel bottle. How would you collect evidence at home to check this fairly?
items.prompt_hi: Tumhara dost kehta hai ki uski nayi bottle paani ko tumhari steel bottle se zyada der thanda rakhti hai. Ghar pe isse fairly check karne ke liye evidence kaise collect karoge?
items.answer: Fill both with the same amount of water from the same cold jug at the same time, keep them in the same place, and after the same time compare how cold the water is (for example, count how long two equal ice cubes last in each). Repeat it a few times.
hints: Ask what must be the same for both bottles
Point to amount of water, starting coldness, place and time
Prompt: keep everything the ___ except the ___
Assert: same water, same place, same time; only the bottle differs; repeat it

verified.solverAnswer: Same amount of water at same starting temperature, same place and time, check temperature at intervals (thermometer/ice), only bottle differs; repeat.

items.prompt_en: Draw a timeline with three boxes showing how the idea of the Earth's shape changed: what people once believed, what evidence was found, and what we know now. Then tell me what each box shows.
items.prompt_hi: Teen box wali ek timeline banao jo dikhaye ki Earth ke shape ka idea kaise badla: log pehle kya maante the, kaunsa evidence mila, aur ab hum kya jaante hain. Phir batao har box kya dikhata hai.
items.answer: Box 1: the Earth is flat. Box 2: evidence such as ships disappearing hull-first, the round shadow of the Earth on the Moon in a lunar eclipse, and travellers sailing all the way around. Box 3: the Earth is round like a ball, confirmed by photos from space.
hints: Invite them to draw the three boxes and arrows first
Point to the middle box as the bridge between the old and new idea
Prompt: old idea flat, evidence ___, new idea ___
Assert: belief, then evidence, then the improved idea of a round Earth

verified.solverAnswer: Box1 old belief flat Earth; box2 evidence like ships disappearing hull first / Earth's shadow on Moon; box3 round Earth.

items.prompt_en: Ravi says, 'Scientists changed their minds about Pluto, so science is just guessing and we can't trust it.' What is wrong with Ravi's thinking?
items.prompt_hi: Ravi kehta hai, 'Scientists ne Pluto ke baare mein apna mann badal liya, matlab science bas guess hai, us pe bharosa nahi kar sakte.' Ravi ki soch mein galti kya hai?
items.answer: The idea changed because of new evidence: scientists found many similar small icy objects far out and made a clearer definition of a planet. Changing an idea when evidence demands it is how science corrects itself and becomes more reliable.
hints: Ask why the scientists changed the name
Point to the discovery of many similar objects beyond Neptune
Prompt: the idea changed because of new ___, which makes science ___
Assert: science updates with evidence; that is a strength, not guessing

verified.solverAnswer: Ideas changing with new evidence is science working, not guessing; Pluto was redefined because many similar objects were found; science self-corrects.

items.prompt_en: Why do scientists repeat an experiment many times and ask other scientists to repeat it too?
items.prompt_hi: Scientists ek experiment ko kai baar kyon dohraate hain aur doosre scientists se bhi dohraane ko kyon kehte hain?
items.answer: One result can be a mistake or just chance. When many repeats, done by different people, give the same result, the evidence becomes much more trustworthy.
hints: Ask what could go wrong if you tried something only once
Point to a mistake like reading the stopwatch late
Prompt: one result can be a ___; many repeats make it more ___
Assert: repeating by many people catches mistakes and builds trust

verified.solverAnswer: To catch mistakes and chance results, check reliability and build trust; others getting the same result makes it more trustworthy.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your younger cousin how science decides which idea to believe. Use one example.
items.prompt_hi: Apne chhote cousin ko samjhao ki science kaise decide karti hai ki kaunsa idea maana jaaye. Ek example ke saath.
items.answer: Science trusts evidence: ideas are tested by observing and experimenting; if new evidence does not fit, the idea is changed. Example: the flat-Earth idea gave way to a round Earth because of ships, eclipse shadows and photos from space.
hints: Invite them to start with 'Science checks ideas by...'
Point to one example they liked, such as the falling balls or the ships
Prompt: we test an idea, and if evidence does not ___, we change the idea
Assert: evidence decides; ideas change when better evidence comes

verified.solverAnswer: Science tests an idea with observation/experiment; if evidence doesn't fit, change the idea; e.g. dropping balls tested heavier-falls-faster.

items.prompt_en: From last time: why did Pluto stop being called a planet?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: Pluto ko planet kehna kyon band kar diya gaya?
items.answer: In 2006 scientists made a clearer definition of a planet after finding many similar small objects far beyond Neptune; Pluto does not clear its path of other objects, so it was called a dwarf planet.
hints: Ask what new name Pluto got
Point to the many similar icy objects found nearby
Prompt: scientists found many ___ objects and made a new ___ of planet
Assert: new discoveries led to a new definition; Pluto is a dwarf planet

verified.solverAnswer: New discoveries of many similar icy objects led to a new definition of planet; Pluto is now a dwarf planet.

workedExample.problem: Meena thinks seeds need light to sprout. Show step by step how she can test this fairly.
steps: Write the idea to test: seeds need light to sprout
Take two identical cups with the same soil and 10 moong seeds in each
Keep everything the same, the water and the warmth, except light: one cup in a dark cupboard, one near a window
Observe and write down what happens every day for five days
Compare: moong seeds sprout in both cups, so light is not needed for sprouting; the evidence, not the guess, decides
fadedVersion: Write the idea to test: seeds need ___ to sprout
Take two identical cups with the same ___ and 10 moong seeds in each
Keep everything the same except ___: one cup in a dark cupboard, one near a window
Observe and ___ what happens every day for five days
Compare: seeds sprout in ___ cups, so the ___ decides

skills.title: Describe how scientists build on each other's work and share methods and results across places and times
Name Indian and world scientists and what they contributed (C.V. Raman, J.C. Bose, Janaki Ammal, Aryabhata, Ibn al-Haytham, Galileo, ISRO teams)
Recognise that anyone who asks questions and collects careful evidence, including farmers, students and citizen scientists, can do science

expectations: Science is built by many people over many centuries and in many countries, each building on earlier work.
Scientists share their methods and results so that others can check, repeat and improve them.

India has a long tradition in science, for example Aryabhata (the Earth spins on its axis), C.V. Raman (scattering of light, Nobel Prize 1930), J.C. Bose (plants respond to their surroundings), Janaki Ammal (better sugarcane varieties) and the teams of ISRO.
Curiosity about everyday things, like why the sea looks blue, can start important discoveries.
Anyone who observes carefully, asks questions and records evidence can contribute, including students and citizen scientists who count birds or record rainfall.

misconceptions.belief: Science is done only by famous people in big laboratories abroad.
signs: Says 'science happens in America, not here'
Cannot imagine a student or farmer doing science
Thinks only Nobel Prize winners are scientists

diagnostic.prompt_en: Who among these can do real science?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inmein se kaun asli science kar sakta hai?

options.text: Only scientists working in big laboratories in other countries
Anyone who asks a question and collects careful evidence, like a student counting birds every morning
Only people who have won a Nobel Prize

remediation.representation: A gallery of photo cards: a farmer saving seeds, a student with a bird notebook, an ISRO engineer, a village health worker
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to find the question and the evidence in each card before saying who is doing science

misconceptions.belief: A great discovery is made by one genius working alone.
signs: Credits a whole mission to one person
Thinks scientists keep their work secret from each other

diagnostic.prompt_en: Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023. Who made it possible?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Chandrayaan-3 2023 mein Chand ke south pole ke paas utra. Ise kisne sambhav banaya?

options.text: One great scientist who built it all alone
Thousands of scientists, engineers and workers sharing work and learning from earlier missions
Only foreign scientists

remediation.representation: A relay-race diagram where each runner is a mission or team passing a baton of knowledge
remediation.moveShape: Have the child name what each earlier runner handed over before the next could run

misconceptions.belief: Science began only in Europe; other cultures, including India, did not contribute.
signs: Says 'India just copied science from the West'
Is surprised that zero and the place-value system came from India

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement is closest to the truth?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsi baat sach ke sabse kareeb hai?

options.text: Science was invented only in Europe
People in India, China, the Arab world, Greece, Africa and elsewhere all added to science
Old Indian knowledge has nothing to do with science

remediation.representation: A world map with pins: place-value and zero (India), Book of Optics (Ibn al-Haytham), telescopes (Galileo), Raman effect (Kolkata)
remediation.moveShape: Let the child place the pins and notice how ideas travelled between places

items.prompt_en: Who was C.V. Raman, and what everyday question did he wonder about on a sea voyage?
items.prompt_hi: C.V. Raman kaun the, aur samudri safar ke dauraan unhone kis rozmarra ke sawaal pe socha?
items.answer: An Indian physicist who wondered why the sea looks blue; his study of how light is scattered led to the Raman effect and the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics.
hints: Ask what colour the sea looked to him from the ship
Point to his question about the colour of the sea
Prompt: he asked why the sea looks ___, and studied how light ___
Assert: Raman studied why the sea looks blue; it led to the Raman effect

verified.solverAnswer: Indian physicist who wondered why the sea looks blue on a voyage; studied scattering of light, Raman effect, Nobel prize 1930.

items.prompt_en: Why do scientists publish and share their results instead of keeping them secret?
items.prompt_hi: Scientists apne results chhupaane ki bajaye publish aur share kyon karte hain?
items.answer: So that others can check and repeat the work and build on it; mistakes get caught and knowledge grows faster.
hints: Ask what happens to a mistake that nobody else ever sees
Point to other scientists repeating the experiment
Prompt: sharing lets others ___ and ___ the work
Assert: sharing lets others check, repeat and build on results

verified.solverAnswer: So others can check, repeat, correct and build on the work; hidden mistakes get found.

items.prompt_en: Raman wondered why the sea looks deep blue. Predict: if you fill a clear glass with tap water and look at it, will the water look blue?
items.prompt_hi: Raman ne socha ki samudra gehra neela kyon dikhta hai. Guess karo: agar ek saaf glass mein nal ka paani bharo, toh kya paani neela dikhega?
items.answer: No, a glass of water looks clear. The blue colour shows only through a great depth of water, because water absorbs some of the red part of sunlight and scatters light so that mostly blue comes back; Raman showed it is not just a reflection of the sky.
hints: Ask for a guess before anyone fills the glass
Point to how little water is in a glass compared with the sea
Prompt: a little water looks ___; only a great ___ of water looks blue
Assert: a glass of water looks clear; deep water looks blue because of how water treats light

verified.solverAnswer: No, a glass of water looks clear/colourless; only a large deep quantity of water looks blue.

items.prompt_en: At exactly noon on the same winter day in January, a student in Kanyakumari and a student in Delhi each measure the shadow of a 1-metre stick. Predict: will the shadows be the same length? What could they learn by sharing their results?
items.prompt_hi: January ke ek hi sardi ke din theek dopahar 12 baje, Kanyakumari ka ek student aur Delhi ka ek student 1 metre lambi chhadi ki parchhai naapte hain. Guess karo: kya dono parchhaiyan barabar hongi? Results share karke wo kya seekh sakte hain?
items.answer: No. Delhi's shadow will be clearly longer because Delhi is farther north and the Sun is lower in its sky. By comparing, they get evidence that the Earth's surface is curved; over 2000 years ago Eratosthenes used this idea to estimate the size of the Earth.
hints: Ask whether the Sun looks equally high everywhere at noon
Point to Delhi being much farther north than Kanyakumari
Prompt: the shadows differ because the Earth's surface is ___
Assert: Delhi's shadow is longer; sharing results shows the Earth is curved

verified.solverAnswer: No, Delhi's shadow longer (Sun lower in sky further north); comparing results shows Earth's surface is curved.

items.prompt_en: Farmers in India have long saved seeds from their best plants and grown them again the next year. Why can this be called a kind of science?
items.prompt_hi: Bharat ke kisaan bahut pehle se apne sabse acche paudhon ke beej bachaakar agle saal phir ugaate aaye hain. Ise ek tarah ka science kyon kaha ja sakta hai?
items.answer: They observe which plants do best, remember or record it, test those seeds again the next season and keep what works: observing, testing and using evidence.
hints: Ask what the farmer notices before choosing seeds
Point to the next season as the test
Prompt: the farmer ___, then ___ again next season, and keeps what works
Assert: observing, testing and keeping what works is a scientific way

verified.solverAnswer: They observe, select, test results over seasons and keep what works: observation, testing, repeating.

items.prompt_en: Compare: Scientist A keeps her discovery secret. Scientist B publishes exactly how she did her experiment so others can repeat it. Whose discovery is more likely to be trusted and improved, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Tulna karo: Scientist A apni khoj chhupa ke rakhti hai. Scientist B bilkul bataati hai ki usne experiment kaise kiya taaki doosre dohra sakein. Kiski khoj pe zyada bharosa hoga aur kiski khoj aage badhegi, aur kyon?
items.answer: Scientist B's, because others can repeat it, check it and build on it; a secret result cannot be checked or improved.
hints: Ask how anyone could check Scientist A's claim
Point to other people repeating B's method
Prompt: B's work can be ___ and ___ by others
Assert: shared work gets checked and improved, so it is trusted more

verified.solverAnswer: Scientist B: others can repeat and check it, find errors and improve it, so more trusted.

items.prompt_en: J.C. Bose built very sensitive instruments to show something surprising about plants. What did he show?
items.prompt_hi: J.C. Bose ne bahut sensitive instruments banaye jo paudhon ke baare mein ek hairaan karne wali baat dikhate the. Unhone kya dikhaya?
items.answer: That plants respond to their surroundings, such as touch, light, heat and injury, and he measured their tiny growth and responses with an instrument called the crescograph.
hints: Ask what people thought plants could not do
Point to his instrument that measured very tiny growth
Prompt: Bose showed that plants ___ to touch, light and heat
Assert: Bose showed plants respond to their surroundings and measured it

verified.solverAnswer: Plants respond to touch, light, heat etc. like living beings; he measured tiny growth/responses (crescograph).

items.prompt_en: Every year, people across India count the birds they see and upload the counts online during bird-count events. How can counts by thousands of ordinary people help scientists?
items.prompt_hi: Har saal poore Bharat mein log bird-count events ke dauraan dikhe hue pakshiyon ko ginkar online daalte hain. Hazaaron aam logon ki ginti scientists ki madad kaise kar sakti hai?
items.answer: Many people in many places give far more data than a few scientists could collect; it shows which birds are increasing or decreasing and where, which helps protect them.
hints: Ask how many places one scientist could visit in a day
Point to thousands of counts from all over the country
Prompt: many people give much more ___ from many ___
Assert: citizen counts give huge data showing which birds need protection

verified.solverAnswer: Huge amounts of data from many places and times show bird numbers/migration/populations that one scientist can't gather; help conservation.

items.prompt_en: Draw a relay race with three runners passing a baton. Label each runner with a person or group who added to our knowledge of the Moon, from long ago to Chandrayaan. Then explain your picture.
items.prompt_hi: Ek relay race banao jismein teen runners baton pass kar rahe hain. Har runner pe kisi aise insaan ya group ka naam likho jisne Chand ke baare mein hamari jaankari badhaayi, bahut pehle se Chandrayaan tak. Phir apni picture samjhao.
items.answer: Runner 1: Aryabhata, who explained that moonlight is reflected sunlight and that eclipses are caused by shadows. Runner 2: Galileo, who saw mountains and craters on the Moon through a telescope. Runner 3: ISRO teams; Chandrayaan-1 found signs of water and Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole. The baton is knowledge passed on.
hints: Invite them to draw the three runners first
Point to the baton as what each runner hands to the next
Prompt: Aryabhata, then ___ with a telescope, then ___ missions
Assert: each runner built on the previous one; knowledge is passed on

verified.solverAnswer: Runners: ancient Indian astronomers like Aryabhata, Galileo with telescope, space agency missions like Chandrayaan; each builds on previous.

items.prompt_en: Tanya says, 'Science is only what scientists in America and Europe did; India just copied.' What is wrong with this?
items.prompt_hi: Tanya kehti hai, 'Science sirf America aur Europe ke scientists ne kiya, India ne bas copy kiya.' Isme galti kya hai?
items.answer: Science has come from many cultures. India gave the place-value number system with zero, Aryabhata's astronomy, Sushruta's ancient surgery text, Raman's discovery and ISRO's missions; scientists everywhere learn from each other.
hints: Ask where our number system with zero came from
Point to Raman, Aryabhata and ISRO
Prompt: India gave ___ and ___ to science
Assert: science comes from many cultures, India included

verified.solverAnswer: Wrong: science came from many cultures; India gave the zero/decimal system, Aryabhata, Raman, Bose, ISRO.

items.prompt_en: Raman did his famous work in Kolkata with simple, low-cost equipment. What does this tell us about doing good science?
items.prompt_hi: Raman ne apna famous kaam Kolkata mein saade, sasta equipment se kiya. Isse acchi science ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: Curiosity, careful observation and clever experiments matter more than expensive laboratories; good science can be done anywhere.
hints: Ask what Raman had that money cannot buy
Point to his question and his careful experiments
Prompt: good science needs ___ and careful ___, not costly labs
Assert: curiosity and careful experiments make good science, anywhere

verified.solverAnswer: Good science needs curiosity and careful experiments, not expensive labs.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend why we call science a 'shared human effort'. Use one example.
items.prompt_hi: Apne dost ko samjhao ki science ko 'insaanon ki saajhi koshish' kyon kehte hain. Ek example do.
items.answer: Many people across countries and centuries add to science, share their results and build on each other's work. Example: knowledge of the Moon grew from Aryabhata to Galileo to ISRO's Chandrayaan missions.
hints: Invite them to start with who adds to science
Point to the relay-race picture
Prompt: people ___ their results and ___ on each other's work
Assert: science grows when many people share and build on work

verified.solverAnswer: Many people share results and build on each other's work across places and time; e.g. Chandrayaan builds on earlier missions.

items.prompt_en: From last time: name one Indian scientist and one thing they discovered or studied.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: ek Indian scientist ka naam batao aur unhone kya khoja ya padha.
items.answer: For example: C.V. Raman studied the scattering of light; J.C. Bose showed plants respond to their surroundings; Janaki Ammal developed better sugarcane varieties; Aryabhata said the Earth spins on its axis; Salim Ali studied birds.
hints: Ask who wondered about the colour of the sea
Point to Raman, Bose or Aryabhata
Prompt: ___ studied ___
Assert: for example, Raman studied how light scatters

verified.solverAnswer: C.V. Raman studied scattering of light (why sea is blue); Bose studied plant responses; Aryabhata astronomy.

workedExample.problem: Trace how knowledge about the cause of malaria grew through the work of different people.
steps: People long ago noticed that fevers were common near swamps and blamed 'bad air' (which is what 'mal aria' means)
In 1880 Alphonse Laveran saw tiny parasites in the blood of malaria patients
In 1897, working in Secunderabad, Ronald Ross found the malaria parasite inside a mosquito
Other scientists showed that a particular kind of mosquito, Anopheles, spreads malaria to people
Doctors and health workers worldwide then used this to fight malaria with nets, medicines and removing standing water
fadedVersion: People long ago noticed fevers near ___ and blamed bad air
In 1880 Laveran saw tiny ___ in the blood of patients
In 1897 in Secunderabad, Ronald Ross found the parasite inside a ___
Other scientists showed that the ___ mosquito spreads it
Health workers used this to fight malaria with ___, medicines and removing standing water

skills.title: Describe acids (sour: lemon, curd, vinegar, tamarind, amla) and bases (bitter, soapy: soap, baking soda) and why unknown substances must never be tasted or touched
Predict and explain litmus colour changes: acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; neutral changes neither
Use turmeric and hibiscus (china rose) indicators to classify substances as acidic, basic or neutral
Explain why indicators, not taste, are used to identify acids and bases, and that strong acids and strong bases are both dangerous

expectations: Acids taste sour (lemon, tamarind, curd, vinegar, amla); bases taste bitter and feel soapy (soap solution, baking soda solution); but unknown substances must never be tasted or touched to test them.
An indicator is a substance that shows a different colour in acidic and in basic solutions.
Litmus (made from lichens): acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; neutral solutions change neither.
Turmeric turns red in a base such as soap solution and stays yellow in acidic and neutral solutions.
Hibiscus (china rose) extract turns dark pink or magenta in acids and green in bases.
Solutions that are neither acidic nor basic, like pure water, sugar solution and common salt solution, are neutral.

misconceptions.belief: All acids are dangerous and burn the skin.
signs: Is afraid to touch lemon juice once told it has acid
Thinks 'acid' always means a lab bottle with a warning sign
Is surprised that curd and tamarind contain acids

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which of these contains an acid?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inmein se kismein acid hai?

options.text: Only the acid bottles in a science laboratory
Lemon juice, curd and tamarind
Nothing that we eat contains acid

remediation.representation: Two-shelf picture: a kitchen shelf of food acids (lemon, curd, imli, vinegar) and a lab shelf of strong acids with warning signs
remediation.moveShape: Sort cards onto the two shelves, then ask what makes the lab shelf dangerous: strength, not the word 'acid'

misconceptions.belief: Tasting is a fine way to test for an acid, and anything acidic will taste sour.
signs: Suggests licking a drop of an unknown liquid
Says 'if it's not sour, it's not an acid'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Your friend finds an unlabelled bottle of clear liquid and wants to taste it to find out if it is an acid. What should she do?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Tumhari dost ko bina label ki ek saaf liquid wali bottle milti hai aur wo use chakh ke dekhna chahti hai ki ye acid hai ya nahi. Use kya karna chahiye?

options.text: Taste a tiny drop; if it is sour, it is an acid
Not taste it at all, and test a drop with an indicator like litmus paper with an adult's help
Smell it deeply and decide

remediation.representation: A safety card: a crossed-out tongue next to a litmus strip
remediation.moveShape: Contrast what taste risks with what a colour strip tells; let the child say which a scientist would choose

misconceptions.belief: The indicator itself makes a substance acidic or basic.
signs: Says 'the litmus made it an acid'
Thinks the substance changed because the paper changed colour

diagnostic.prompt_en: Blue litmus turns red when dipped in lemon juice. What does this tell us?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Neela litmus nimbu ke ras mein daalne pe laal ho jaata hai. Isse kya pata chalta hai?

options.text: The litmus turned the lemon juice into an acid
The lemon juice was already acidic; the litmus only showed it
The lemon juice has now become neutral

remediation.representation: A 'detective' picture: the indicator as a detective that reports, not a magician that changes
remediation.moveShape: Test the same lemon juice twice with two different indicators; ask whether two different papers could both 'make' it acidic

misconceptions.belief: Bases are always safe because they are the 'opposite' of acids.
signs: Says soap is a base so all bases must be gentle
Ignores warning labels on drain cleaners

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement is true?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsi baat sahi hai?

options.text: Bases are always safe to touch
Some bases, like the caustic soda in drain cleaners, can burn skin just like strong acids
Only acids can ever be harmful

remediation.representation: A warning-label gallery: a drain-cleaner packet next to a toilet-acid bottle, both with gloves symbols
remediation.moveShape: Ask what the two labels have in common, then link danger to strength rather than to acid or base

items.prompt_en: Name three things in your kitchen that taste sour. What type of substance are they?
items.prompt_hi: Apne kitchen ki teen khatti cheezein batao. Ye kis tarah ke padarth hain?
items.answer: For example lemon, tamarind, curd, vinegar, amla, raw mango or tomato; they are acidic (they contain acids).
hints: Ask what they add to make chaat or rasam tangy
Point to lemon, imli and dahi
Prompt: sour foods contain ___
Assert: lemon, imli and curd are sour because they contain acids

verified.solverAnswer: Lemon, tamarind, curd/vinegar; they are acids.

items.prompt_en: What colour does blue litmus turn in an acid, and what colour does red litmus turn in a base?
items.prompt_hi: Neela litmus acid mein kis rang ka ho jaata hai, aur laal litmus base mein kis rang ka?
items.answer: Blue litmus turns red in an acid; red litmus turns blue in a base.
acceptable: blue to red in acid, red to blue in base
acid mein laal, base mein neela
hints: Ask them to picture lemon juice touching blue paper
Point to the litmus going the 'opposite' colour each time
Prompt: acid turns blue litmus ___; base turns red litmus ___
Assert: acid makes blue litmus red; base makes red litmus blue

verified.solverAnswer: Blue litmus turns red in acid; red litmus turns blue in base.

items.prompt_en: Mix a pinch of haldi in a little water and wipe it on a strip of white paper to make it yellow. Predict: what will happen when you touch it with soap water? And with lemon juice?
items.prompt_hi: Thodi haldi paani mein milaao aur safed kaagaz ki patti pe laga ke use peela kar do. Guess karo: is pe sabun ka paani lagaoge toh kya hoga? Aur nimbu ka ras lagaoge toh?
items.answer: With soap water it turns red (reddish-brown) because soap is basic; with lemon juice it stays yellow, because turmeric does not change colour in an acid.
acceptable: red with soap, yellow with lemon
hints: Ask for a guess for each liquid before testing
Point to which of the two feels soapy and which tastes sour
Prompt: turmeric turns ___ in a base and stays ___ in an acid
Assert: soap turns haldi red; lemon leaves it yellow

verified.solverAnswer: Soap water turns haldi paper red/reddish-brown; lemon juice leaves it yellow.

items.prompt_en: Soak a few red hibiscus (gudhal) petals in warm water until the water turns coloured. Predict the colour when you add a few drops of it to (a) lemon juice and (b) baking soda solution.
items.prompt_hi: Laal gudhal ke kuch petals garam paani mein bhigo do jab tak paani rangeen na ho jaaye. Guess karo, iski kuch boondein (a) nimbu ke ras mein aur (b) baking soda ke ghol mein daalne pe kya rang aayega?
items.answer: (a) In lemon juice it turns dark pink or magenta because lemon juice is acidic. (b) In baking soda solution it turns green because baking soda solution is basic.
acceptable: pink in lemon, green in baking soda
hints: Ask which of the two is the acid and which is the base
Point to hibiscus showing two very different colours
Prompt: hibiscus turns ___ in acid and ___ in base
Assert: dark pink in lemon juice, green in baking soda solution

verified.solverAnswer: (a) lemon juice: dark pink/red; (b) baking soda: green.

items.prompt_en: Predict: will sugar solution change the colour of turmeric paper, blue litmus or red litmus? What does your prediction tell you about sugar solution?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: kya cheeni ka ghol haldi wale kaagaz, neele litmus ya laal litmus ka rang badlega? Isse cheeni ke ghol ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: None of them changes colour, because sugar solution is neutral: neither acidic nor basic.
hints: Ask whether sugar water tastes sour or feels soapy
Point to what 'no change in any indicator' means
Prompt: if no indicator changes, the solution is ___
Assert: sugar solution changes no indicator, so it is neutral

verified.solverAnswer: No change in any; sugar solution is neutral.

items.prompt_en: Why do scientists use indicators instead of tasting substances to find out whether they are acids or bases?
items.prompt_hi: Scientists acid ya base pata karne ke liye chakhne ki bajaye indicators kyon use karte hain?
items.answer: Tasting or touching unknown substances can be dangerous because strong acids and bases burn and some substances are poisonous; indicators show the type safely through a colour change.
hints: Ask what could happen if the unknown liquid were a strong acid
Point to the colour change as a safe signal
Prompt: tasting can ___ us, while indicators show the type by ___
Assert: indicators are safe; tasting unknown chemicals can harm us

verified.solverAnswer: Tasting unknown chemicals can be harmful; indicators show type safely by colour change.

items.prompt_en: Two clear liquids, A and B. Liquid A turns blue litmus red. Liquid B turns red litmus blue. Which could be vinegar and which could be soap solution? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Do saaf liquid hain, A aur B. A neele litmus ko laal karta hai. B laal litmus ko neela karta hai. Inmein se kaun sirka ho sakta hai aur kaun sabun ka paani? Kyon?
items.answer: A could be vinegar, because acids turn blue litmus red; B could be soap solution, because bases turn red litmus blue.
acceptable: a is vinegar, b is soap
hints: Ask which change happens with an acid
Point to the blue-to-red change for A
Prompt: A is the ___ (vinegar); B is the ___ (soap)
Assert: A is acidic like vinegar; B is basic like soap solution

verified.solverAnswer: A (turns blue litmus red) = acid like vinegar; B (turns red litmus blue) = base like soap solution.

items.prompt_en: Kabir writes in his notebook: 'Lime water turned red litmus blue, so lime water is an acid.' Find the mistake.
items.prompt_hi: Kabir apni copy mein likhta hai: 'Choone ke paani ne laal litmus ko neela kar diya, isliye choone ka paani acid hai.' Galti dhoondo.
items.answer: Turning red litmus blue shows a base, not an acid; lime water is basic.
hints: Ask what an acid does to litmus
Point to red litmus turning blue
Prompt: red litmus turning blue means the substance is a ___
Assert: lime water is a base, because it turns red litmus blue

verified.solverAnswer: Turning red litmus blue shows a base, not an acid; lime water is basic.

items.prompt_en: Make a three-column table with the headings acidic, basic and neutral. Place these by their indicator results: lemon juice, soap solution, sugar water, baking soda solution, vinegar, salt water. Say how you decided each one.
items.prompt_hi: Teen column wali table banao: acidic, basic aur neutral. Inhe indicator ke result ke hisaab se rakho: nimbu ka ras, sabun ka paani, cheeni ka paani, baking soda ka ghol, sirka, namak ka paani. Har ek ke liye batao kaise decide kiya.
items.answer: Acidic: lemon juice and vinegar (turn blue litmus red, hibiscus pink). Basic: soap solution and baking soda solution (turn red litmus blue, turmeric red, hibiscus green). Neutral: sugar water and salt water (no indicator changes).
hints: Invite them to draw the three columns first
Point to one indicator result at a time
Prompt: lemon and vinegar go under ___; soap and baking soda under ___
Assert: acidic lemon and vinegar, basic soap and baking soda, neutral sugar and salt water

verified.solverAnswer: Acidic: lemon juice, vinegar; basic: soap solution, baking soda solution; neutral: sugar water, salt water (by no change in indicators).

items.prompt_en: Your aunt's red cabbage sabzi turned bluish-green when a pinch of baking soda (khane ka soda) went into it. What does this tell you about red cabbage?
items.prompt_hi: Tumhari chachi ki laal patta gobhi ki sabzi mein chutki bhar khane ka soda gaya aur wo neeli-hari ho gayi. Isse laal patta gobhi ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: Red cabbage contains a natural indicator: it changes to blue-green or green in a base such as baking soda (and turns pinkish-red in an acid).
hints: Ask whether baking soda is an acid or a base
Point to the colour change as the clue
Prompt: red cabbage acts as an ___ that turns green in a ___
Assert: red cabbage is a natural indicator that turns green in a base

verified.solverAnswer: Red cabbage is a natural indicator, turns bluish-green in a base like baking soda.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your younger sister how she could find out, without tasting, whether a mystery clear liquid is acidic, basic or neutral, using only haldi paper and gudhal water.
items.prompt_hi: Apni chhoti behen ko samjhao ki bina chakhe, sirf haldi wale kaagaz aur gudhal ke paani se, wo kaise pata kar sakti hai ki ek anjaan saaf liquid acidic hai, basic hai ya neutral.
items.answer: Put a drop on haldi paper: if it turns red, the liquid is basic. If it stays yellow, it is acidic or neutral, so test with gudhal water: dark pink means acidic, no change from its own colour means neutral, and green would mean basic.
hints: Invite them to start with the haldi test
Point to what haldi cannot tell apart
Prompt: haldi red means ___; if still yellow, gudhal pink means ___
Assert: haldi finds bases; gudhal separates acids from neutral

verified.solverAnswer: Dab haldi paper: turns red means base; if still yellow, add gudhal: pink/red means acid, no change/unchanged colour means neutral.

items.prompt_en: Quick recall from last time: which indicator turns red in soap solution, and which indicator turns red in lemon juice?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se jaldi batao: kaunsa indicator sabun ke paani mein laal hota hai, aur kaunsa nimbu ke ras mein laal hota hai?
items.answer: Turmeric turns red in soap solution (a base); blue litmus turns red in lemon juice (an acid).
hints: Ask which test they did with the yellow paper
Point to blue litmus in an acid
Prompt: ___ turns red in soap; ___ litmus turns red in lemon
Assert: haldi goes red in soap; blue litmus goes red in lemon juice

verified.solverAnswer: Haldi (turmeric) turns red in soap; blue litmus turns red in lemon juice.
verified.note: HINT LEAK (partial): hint 2 ('Point to blue litmus in an acid') gives half of the answer.

items.prompt_en: Drain-cleaning powder contains caustic soda, which is a base. Why does its packet warn you to wear gloves, if bases are the 'opposite' of acids?
items.prompt_hi: Naali saaf karne wale powder mein caustic soda hota hai, jo ek base hai. Agar base acid ka 'ulta' hai, toh iske packet pe gloves pehenne ki warning kyon hoti hai?
items.answer: Strong bases are corrosive too and can burn skin and eyes, just like strong acids; 'opposite' in chemistry does not mean 'safe'.
hints: Ask whether being opposite means being gentle
Point to the gloves symbol on both acid and base cleaners
Prompt: strong ___ can burn skin just like strong acids
Assert: strong bases are dangerous too; that is why gloves are needed

verified.solverAnswer: Strong bases like caustic soda are corrosive and can burn skin like strong acids; opposite doesn't mean harmless.

workedExample.problem: Find out whether a solution of washing soda is acidic, basic or neutral, using turmeric paper and hibiscus water. (An adult prepares the solution.)
steps: Put a drop of the solution on turmeric paper: it turns red
Turmeric turns red only in a base, so the solution is likely basic
Check with hibiscus water: a few drops of it in the solution turn green
Hibiscus turns green in a base, so both indicators agree
Conclusion: washing soda solution is basic; we found this without tasting or touching it
fadedVersion: Put a drop of the solution on turmeric paper: it turns ___
Turmeric turns red only in a ___, so the solution is likely basic
Check with hibiscus water: it turns ___
Hibiscus turns green in a base, so both ___ agree
Conclusion: washing soda solution is ___; we found this without ___ it

skills.title: Explain neutralisation: an acid and a base react and cancel each other's effect, forming a salt and water and giving out heat
Use an indicator to follow neutralisation and tell neutralising apart from simply diluting
Apply neutralisation to daily life: antacids, ant bites, soil treatment, toothpaste and treating factory waste

expectations: When an acid and a base are mixed in the right amounts, they cancel each other's effect; this is called neutralisation.
Neutralisation forms a salt and water, and heat is given out.
An indicator shows neutralisation happening: hibiscus water that is pink in an acid loses its pink as a base is added, and turns green once there is extra base.
Adding water only dilutes an acid; it stays acidic. A base is needed to neutralise it.

Uses: antacids (mild bases such as milk of magnesia) for too much stomach acid; baking soda on an ant bite (ants inject formic acid); lime (chuna) on acidic soil; toothpaste (basic) against acids made in the mouth; neutralising acidic factory waste before it reaches rivers.
The products of neutralisation are usually not harmful; common salt itself can be made by neutralising hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide.

misconceptions.belief: Mixing an acid and a base always produces something harmful.
signs: Says 'never mix acids and bases, it makes poison'
Is surprised that antacids work by mixing a base with acid

diagnostic.prompt_en: When hydrochloric acid is neutralised by exactly the right amount of sodium hydroxide, what forms?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Jab hydrochloric acid ko bilkul sahi maatra mein sodium hydroxide se neutralise karte hain, toh kya banta hai?

options.text: A dangerous, stronger acid
Common salt and water
A poisonous gas, every time

remediation.representation: A balance-scale picture: acid on one side, base on the other, levelling out into 'salt + water' in the middle
remediation.moveShape: Show the antacid example first, then ask whether the doctor would give something that makes poison

misconceptions.belief: Adding plain water to an acid neutralises it.
signs: Says 'just add lots of water and the acid becomes neutral'
Confuses weaker with neutral

diagnostic.prompt_en: Shreya adds a lot of plain water to some lemon juice. Is the lemon juice now neutral?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Shreya thode se nimbu ke ras mein bahut saara saada paani daal deti hai. Kya ab nimbu ka ras neutral ho gaya?

options.text: Yes, water neutralises acids
No, it is still acidic, only weaker; a base is needed to neutralise it
It turns into a base

remediation.representation: Two glasses with hibiscus drops: diluted lemon juice still pink, lemon juice with baking soda no longer pink
remediation.moveShape: Let the child predict both colours, then compare 'weaker' and 'cancelled'

misconceptions.belief: Adding more and more base just keeps a solution neutral; you can never add too much.
signs: Says 'the more antacid, the better'
Expects the colour to stop changing once neutral

diagnostic.prompt_en: Hibiscus water in lemon juice is pink. Mohan keeps adding baking soda solution even after the pink has gone. What happens?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Nimbu ke ras mein gudhal ka paani gulaabi hai. Mohan gulaabi rang jaane ke baad bhi baking soda ka ghol daalta jaata hai. Kya hoga?

options.text: It stays neutral no matter how much base is added
It becomes basic, and the hibiscus turns green
It turns back into an acid

remediation.representation: A colour strip from pink through the neutral colour to green, with a slider for 'drops of base'
remediation.moveShape: Slide past the neutral point and ask the child to name what the green means

items.prompt_en: What do we call the reaction in which an acid and a base cancel each other's effect?
items.prompt_hi: Jab acid aur base ek doosre ka asar khatam kar dete hain, us reaction ko kya kehte hain?
items.answer: Neutralisation.
hints: Ask what word sounds like 'making neutral'
Point to the word neutral inside it
Prompt: acid + base cancelling is called ___
Assert: it is called neutralisation

verified.solverAnswer: Neutralisation.

items.prompt_en: What two things are formed when an acid neutralises a base? What else is given out?
items.prompt_hi: Jab acid aur base ka neutralisation hota hai toh kaunsi do cheezein banti hain? Aur kya nikalta hai?
items.answer: A salt and water are formed, and heat is given out.
hints: Ask what common substance is made from an acid and a base
Point to the warming of the mixture
Prompt: acid + base gives ___ + ___, and ___ is given out
Assert: salt and water form, and heat is released

verified.solverAnswer: Salt and water are formed, and heat is given out.

items.prompt_en: Add a few drops of hibiscus water to some lemon juice: it turns pink. Now add baking soda solution little by little, stirring. Predict what you will see happen.
items.prompt_hi: Thode nimbu ke ras mein gudhal ke paani ki kuch boondein daalo: wo gulaabi ho jaata hai. Ab dheere dheere baking soda ka ghol daalte aur hilaate jao. Guess karo kya hota dikhega?
items.answer: It fizzes with bubbles of carbon dioxide; the pink slowly fades as the acid is neutralised, and when extra baking soda is added it turns green because the mixture has become basic.
hints: Ask for a guess about both bubbles and colour
Point to what pink means and what green means
Prompt: pink fades as the acid is ___, and turns ___ with extra base
Assert: fizzing, pink fading, then green once base is in excess

verified.solverAnswer: Fizzing/bubbles (CO2), pink fades as acid used up, then turns green when baking soda is in excess.

items.prompt_en: An ant bite stings because the ant injects formic acid. Predict whether rubbing on (a) lemon juice or (b) a paste of baking soda would give relief, and why.
items.prompt_hi: Cheenti ke kaatne pe jalan isliye hoti hai kyonki cheenti formic acid daalti hai. Guess karo, (a) nimbu ka ras ya (b) baking soda ka paste lagaane se aaraam milega, aur kyon?
items.answer: The baking soda paste, because it is a base and neutralises the acid; lemon juice is itself an acid and would not neutralise it.
hints: Ask whether formic acid needs more acid or a base
Point to baking soda being basic
Prompt: an acid sting needs a ___ to neutralise it
Assert: baking soda, a base, neutralises the formic acid

verified.solverAnswer: (b) baking soda paste: a base neutralises the formic acid; lemon adds more acid.

items.prompt_en: Why might a doctor suggest an antacid such as milk of magnesia when someone has acidity, a burning feeling after a heavy, spicy meal?
items.prompt_hi: Bhaari, teekha khaana khaane ke baad kisi ko acidity, yaani jalan, ho toh doctor milk of magnesia jaisa antacid kyon dete hain?
items.answer: The stomach makes hydrochloric acid to digest food; too much of it causes the burning. An antacid is a mild base that neutralises the extra acid.
hints: Ask what the stomach makes to help digestion
Point to the antacid being a mild base
Prompt: the antacid is a ___ that ___ the extra stomach acid
Assert: a mild base in the antacid neutralises excess stomach acid

verified.solverAnswer: Stomach has excess acid; antacid is a mild base that neutralises it.

items.prompt_en: Compare: Glass A has lemon juice with a lot of water added. Glass B has lemon juice with just the right amount of baking soda added. Which one has been neutralised? How would hibiscus water tell you?
items.prompt_hi: Tulna karo: Glass A mein nimbu ke ras mein bahut paani daala gaya. Glass B mein nimbu ke ras mein bilkul sahi maatra mein baking soda daala gaya. Kiska neutralisation hua? Gudhal ka paani ye kaise bataayega?
items.answer: Glass B is neutralised; glass A is only diluted and still acidic. Hibiscus water turns pink in A but shows no pink in B.
hints: Ask whether water is a base
Point to the hibiscus colour in each glass
Prompt: A is only ___; B has been ___
Assert: B is neutralised; A is just weaker acid and still turns hibiscus pink

verified.solverAnswer: B is neutralised (acid+base); A is only diluted, still acidic and turns hibiscus pink (just a weaker colour). Hibiscus: pink = acid, green = base.

items.prompt_en: A farmer's soil test shows that his soil is too acidic for his crop. What could he add to it, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Ek kisaan ki mitti ki jaanch se pata chalta hai ki mitti fasal ke liye bahut acidic hai. Wo usme kya mila sakta hai, aur kyon?
items.answer: Quicklime or slaked lime (chuna), which is a base, to neutralise the acid in the soil.
hints: Ask what kind of substance cancels an acid
Point to chuna, used to whitewash walls
Prompt: he adds a ___ like chuna to ___ the soil
Assert: lime, a base, neutralises acidic soil

verified.solverAnswer: Add lime (chuna/calcium hydroxide/quicklime), a base, to neutralise the acidic soil.

items.prompt_en: Why does brushing your teeth after eating sweets help protect them? Use the idea of acids and bases.
items.prompt_hi: Meetha khaane ke baad brush karne se daant kyon bachte hain? Acid aur base ka idea use karke samjhao.
items.answer: Bacteria in the mouth break down sugary food left on the teeth and make acids that damage the tooth enamel. Toothpaste is basic and neutralises these acids, and brushing removes the leftover food.
hints: Ask what bacteria make from leftover sugar
Point to toothpaste being basic
Prompt: bacteria make ___; toothpaste, a ___, neutralises it
Assert: toothpaste neutralises the acid bacteria make from sugar

verified.solverAnswer: Bacteria turn leftover sugar into acids that harm tooth enamel; toothpaste is basic and neutralises the acid.

items.prompt_en: Anu says, 'Never mix an acid with a base; it always makes poison.' What would you tell Anu?
items.prompt_hi: Anu kehti hai, 'Acid ko kabhi base ke saath mat milao, isse hamesha zeher banta hai.' Tum Anu ko kya bataoge?
items.answer: Neutralisation usually gives a salt and water, which are often harmless, for example common salt and water; we use it safely in antacids and for ant bites. Strong acids and bases are dangerous to handle themselves.
hints: Ask what an antacid does inside the stomach
Point to the products of neutralisation
Prompt: acid + base usually gives ___ and ___
Assert: neutralisation gives salt and water and is used safely every day

verified.solverAnswer: Not always poison; acid+base gives salt and water, used safely (antacids, ant bite remedies); but strong ones should not be mixed carelessly.

items.prompt_en: Draw a colour strip of four boxes showing hibiscus water in: lemon juice alone, lemon juice with a little baking soda, lemon juice with just enough baking soda, and lemon juice with too much baking soda. Label each box acidic, neutral or basic.
items.prompt_hi: Chaar box wali ek colour strip banao jo dikhaye gudhal ka paani: sirf nimbu ke ras mein, thode baking soda ke saath, bilkul sahi maatra ke saath, aur bahut zyada baking soda ke saath. Har box pe acidic, neutral ya basic likho.
items.answer: Box 1: dark pink, acidic. Box 2: lighter pink, still acidic. Box 3: the extract's own purplish colour with no pink, neutral. Box 4: green, basic.
hints: Invite them to colour the first and last boxes first
Point to the middle box as the balancing point
Prompt: pink is ___, green is ___, in between is ___
Assert: pink acidic, fading pink still acidic, no pink neutral, green basic

verified.solverAnswer: Box1 pink acidic; box2 paler pink still acidic; box3 no pink/original colour neutral; box4 green basic.

items.prompt_en: Factories must treat acidic waste water with a base before letting it flow into a river. Why?
items.prompt_hi: Factories ko acidic gande paani ko nadi mein chhodne se pehle base se treat karna padta hai. Kyon?
items.answer: Acidic water would harm fish, water plants and the people and animals who use the river; neutralising it with a base makes it much safer before release.
hints: Ask who lives in and drinks from the river
Point to the base cancelling the acid
Prompt: acidic waste would ___ river life, so it is ___ first
Assert: neutralising factory waste protects living things in the river

verified.solverAnswer: Acidic waste would harm fish/plants and river life; base neutralises it so it is safe to release.

items.prompt_en: Teach your friend what neutralisation is, with one example from home and one from a farm.
items.prompt_hi: Apne dost ko sikhao ki neutralisation kya hota hai, ek example ghar se aur ek khet se.
items.answer: Neutralisation is when an acid and a base cancel each other's effect, forming salt and water and giving out heat. Home: baking soda on an ant bite or an antacid for acidity. Farm: adding lime to acidic soil.
hints: Invite them to start with acid plus base
Point to the ant bite and the farmer's soil
Prompt: acid + base gives ___ + water; at home ___, on the farm ___
Assert: acid and base cancel; ant bite at home, lime on acidic soil

verified.solverAnswer: Neutralisation: acid and base react to give salt and water. Home: baking soda on ant bite (formic acid) or antacid; farm: lime on acidic soil.

items.prompt_en: From last time: why is baking soda rubbed on an ant bite?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: cheenti ke kaatne pe baking soda kyon lagaate hain?
items.answer: The ant injects formic acid; baking soda is a base that neutralises it.
hints: Ask what the ant puts into the skin
Point to baking soda being basic
Prompt: baking soda, a ___, neutralises the formic ___
Assert: baking soda neutralises the ant's formic acid

verified.solverAnswer: Baking soda is a base and neutralises the ant's formic acid.

workedExample.problem: Riya has acidity after a spicy meal. Explain step by step what an antacid does.
steps: The stomach makes hydrochloric acid to help digest food
Too much acid causes a burning feeling, which we call acidity
An antacid such as milk of magnesia contains a mild base
The base reacts with the extra acid: this is neutralisation
Salt and water form, the extra acid is used up, and the burning eases
fadedVersion: The stomach makes ___ acid to help digest food
Too much acid causes a burning feeling called ___
An antacid such as milk of magnesia contains a mild ___
The base reacts with the extra acid: this is ___
___ and water form, and the burning eases

skills.title: Identify the terminals of an electric cell (positive metal cap, negative flat disc) and the parts of a torch bulb (filament and two terminals)
Build a closed circuit by joining each terminal of the bulb to a different terminal of the cell in one complete loop
Explain that current flows only around a complete, closed path, in one direction, and is not used up by the bulb
Join cells into a battery (positive of one to negative of the next) and explain why only cells, never wall sockets, are used for experiments

expectations: An electric cell has two terminals: a positive (+) terminal, the metal cap, and a negative (−) terminal, the flat metal base.
A torch bulb has a thin coiled wire called the filament joined to two terminals; current must go in at one terminal and come out at the other.
The bulb glows only when there is a complete, unbroken path from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal: a closed circuit.
If the path is broken anywhere (a loose wire, an open switch, a broken filament) the circuit is open and no current flows anywhere in it.
Current flows one way around the whole loop and is the same all the way round; the bulb does not use up current. The energy stored in the cell is what gets used up over time.
Cells are safe for experiments; electricity from wall sockets (about 230 volts in India) can kill and must never be used for experiments.

misconceptions.belief: One wire from the cell to the bulb is enough to make it glow.
signs: Connects only the positive terminal to the bulb and expects light
Draws a single wire like a hose pipe carrying electricity to the bulb

diagnostic.prompt_en: A wire goes from the + terminal of a cell to the bottom tip of a bulb. Nothing is joined to the − terminal. Will the bulb glow?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek taar cell ke + terminal se bulb ke neeche wale tip tak jaata hai. − terminal se kuch nahi juda. Kya bulb jalega?

options.text: Yes, one wire is enough to carry electricity to the bulb
No, there must be a complete loop back to the other terminal of the cell
Only if the wire is very thick

remediation.representation: An animated loop of moving dots that stops dead wherever the path has a gap
remediation.moveShape: Let the child break and close the loop on screen at different places and say where the dots stop

misconceptions.belief: The bulb uses up current, so less current comes back to the cell.
signs: Says the wire after the bulb carries 'less electricity'
Expects a second bulb further along the loop to be dimmer

diagnostic.prompt_en: If we could measure the current in the wire going into a glowing bulb and in the wire coming out of it, what would we find?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Agar hum jalte bulb mein jaane wale taar aur usse nikalne wale taar, dono ka current naap sakein, toh kya milega?

options.text: Less current comes out, because the bulb used some up
The same current goes in and comes out
No current comes out at all

remediation.representation: A chain-of-people model: a rope loop passed hand to hand that warms one person's palms (the bulb) without getting shorter
remediation.moveShape: Ask what got 'used up' in the model: the rope or the pulling effort; map rope to current and effort to the cell's energy

misconceptions.belief: Current comes out of both terminals of the cell and clashes in the bulb to make light.
signs: Draws arrows from both ends of the cell pointing towards the bulb
Says the two currents 'meet' or 'crash' in the filament

diagnostic.prompt_en: How does current flow in a circuit with one cell and one bulb?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek cell aur ek bulb wale circuit mein current kaise behta hai?

options.text: Current comes out of both ends of the cell and meets in the bulb to make light
Current flows one way around the loop: out of one terminal, through the bulb, back into the other terminal
Current stays inside the cell

remediation.representation: An LED tester that lights only one way round, shown next to the arrow diagram
remediation.moveShape: Flip the LED and ask why it goes dark if current came from both ends anyway

items.prompt_en: An electric cell has a small metal cap at one end and a flat metal disc at the other. Which is the positive terminal and which is the negative?
items.prompt_hi: Ek electric cell ke ek sire pe chhota metal cap hai aur doosre pe chapti metal disc. Kaunsa positive terminal hai aur kaunsa negative?
items.answer: The metal cap is the positive (+) terminal; the flat metal disc is the negative (−) terminal.
hints: Ask them to look for a + sign printed near one end of a cell
Point to the raised metal cap
Prompt: the cap is the ___ terminal and the flat end is the ___
Assert: cap is positive, flat disc is negative

verified.solverAnswer: Metal cap is the positive (+) terminal; flat disc is negative (-).

items.prompt_en: You have one cell, one torch bulb and two wires. Describe how to connect them so that the bulb glows.
items.prompt_hi: Tumhare paas ek cell, ek torch bulb aur do taar hain. Batao inhe kaise jodoge ki bulb jal jaaye.
items.answer: Join one wire from the + terminal to one terminal of the bulb (for example its metal side), and the other wire from the bulb's other terminal (the tip at its base) to the − terminal, making one complete loop.
acceptable: plus to bulb, bulb to minus
hints: Ask how many terminals the bulb has
Point to each wire needing a different cell terminal
Prompt: + terminal to one bulb terminal, other bulb terminal to the ___ terminal
Assert: each bulb terminal to a different cell terminal, forming a closed loop

verified.solverAnswer: Connect one wire from cell + to one bulb terminal (base tip), the other wire from the bulb's other terminal (side) to cell -, making a closed loop.

items.prompt_en: Predict before you try: a wire joins the cell's + terminal to the bulb's base tip, but the cell's − terminal is not joined to anything. Will the bulb glow?
items.prompt_hi: Try karne se pehle guess karo: ek taar cell ke + terminal ko bulb ke neeche ke tip se jodta hai, par cell ka − terminal kisi se nahi juda. Kya bulb jalega?
items.answer: No. The path is not complete; current needs a closed loop that goes back to the other terminal of the cell.
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason first
Point to where the current could go after the bulb
Prompt: current needs a ___ path back to the ___ terminal
Assert: no glow, because the loop is not closed

verified.solverAnswer: No, loop not complete.

items.prompt_en: Two identical bulbs are joined one after the other in a single loop with a cell. Predict: will the second bulb, the one the current reaches 'later', be dimmer than the first?
items.prompt_hi: Do bilkul ek jaise bulb ek hi loop mein ek ke baad ek cell ke saath jode gaye. Guess karo: kya doosra bulb, jahaan current 'baad mein' pahunchta hai, pehle se kam jalega?
items.answer: No, both glow equally brightly, because the same current flows through both; current is not used up along the loop. (Both are dimmer than one bulb alone would be.)
hints: Ask whether current gets 'eaten' on the way round
Point to the single loop with nowhere for current to leak out
Prompt: the ___ current flows through both bulbs, so they glow ___
Assert: both glow equally; the current is the same all round

verified.solverAnswer: No, both glow equally; the same current flows through both in a single loop.

items.prompt_en: A torch needs two cells. Predict: will it light if one cell is put in the wrong way round, so that both + ends face each other?
items.prompt_hi: Ek torch mein do cell lagte hain. Guess karo: agar ek cell ulta lag jaaye, yaani dono + sire aamne-saamne hon, toh kya torch jalegi?
items.answer: No (or only very faintly): the two cells push current in opposite directions and cancel each other. Cells must be joined + to −.
hints: Ask which way each cell tries to push the current
Point to the two + ends touching
Prompt: the cells push in ___ directions and ___ each other
Assert: it will not light; cells must be joined positive to negative

verified.solverAnswer: No, it won't light; cells must be connected + to - so they push the same way.

items.prompt_en: A torch bulb looks fine from outside but does not glow, even with new cells. Why might that be?
items.prompt_hi: Torch ka bulb bahar se theek dikhta hai par naye cell daalne pe bhi nahi jalta. Aisa kyon ho sakta hai?
items.answer: Its filament may be broken (the bulb has fused), so the path through the bulb is broken and the circuit is open; or a contact may be loose.
hints: Ask what thin part inside the bulb must carry the current
Point to the filament
Prompt: if the ___ is broken, the circuit is ___
Assert: a broken filament opens the circuit, so no current flows

verified.solverAnswer: Filament may be broken (fused), so the circuit is open; or poor contact.

items.prompt_en: Arjun says current comes out of both ends of the cell and crashes together in the bulb to make light. Meera says current flows one way round the whole loop. Who is right, and what could show it?
items.prompt_hi: Arjun kehta hai current cell ke dono siron se nikal ke bulb mein takraata hai aur roshni banti hai. Meera kehti hai current poore loop mein ek hi disha mein behta hai. Kaun sahi hai, aur ye kaise dikha sakte hain?
items.answer: Meera is right. An LED lights only when it is joined one particular way round, which shows current has one direction; the same current flows all around the loop.
hints: Ask what would happen to an LED if current came from both ends anyway
Point to the LED that lights only one way
Prompt: current flows in ___ direction around the loop
Assert: Meera is right; an LED shows current has one direction

verified.solverAnswer: Meera; current flows one way round the loop; an LED lights only when connected one way round.

items.prompt_en: Inside a torch there are no loose wires. What parts complete the circuit instead?
items.prompt_hi: Torch ke andar khule taar nahi hote. Unki jagah circuit ko kaun poora karta hai?
items.answer: Metal strips, the spring and the metal body or case, along with the switch, connect the cells' terminals to the bulb, forming a closed loop when the switch is on.
hints: Ask what material the inside strips are made of
Point to the spring touching the last cell
Prompt: ___ strips and the spring act like the ___
Assert: metal strips, spring and switch make the loop instead of wires

verified.solverAnswer: Metal strips/springs and the switch inside the torch complete the circuit in place of wires.

items.prompt_en: Why is it safe to do circuit experiments with torch cells but never with the plug socket at home?
items.prompt_hi: Torch ke cell se circuit experiment karna safe kyon hai, par ghar ke plug socket se kabhi nahi?
items.answer: A cell gives a small voltage (about 1.5 V) that cannot push dangerous current through our body; the mains is about 230 V and can push enough current through the body to cause a severe shock or death.
acceptable: socket se jaan ja sakti hai
hints: Ask how many volts a torch cell gives
Point to the mains being about 150 times more
Prompt: a cell is about ___ V, the mains about ___ V
Assert: cells are safe; mains electricity can kill, so never experiment with it

verified.solverAnswer: Cells are low voltage (about 1.5 V) and safe; mains (230 V) can cause fatal shock.

items.prompt_en: Riddhi's worksheet says: 'The bulb glows because electricity comes from the bulb and goes into the cell.' Spot the mistake.
items.prompt_hi: Riddhi ki worksheet mein likha hai: 'Bulb isliye jalta hai kyonki bijli bulb se nikal ke cell mein jaati hai.' Galti pakdo.
items.answer: The cell is the source: it pushes current around the circuit through the bulb. The bulb does not make electricity; it changes electrical energy into light and heat.
hints: Ask which part runs out when the torch gets dim
Point to the cell as the part that gets replaced
Prompt: the ___ is the source; the bulb changes energy into ___
Assert: the cell drives the current; the bulb turns it into light

verified.solverAnswer: Current flows from cell through bulb and back to the cell around the loop; cell is the source, bulb turns electrical energy into light and heat; not from bulb into cell.

items.prompt_en: Look at four set-ups: (A) one wire from + to the bulb's tip; (B) both wires from the cell touching only the bulb's tip; (C) one wire from + to the bulb's side, another from the bulb's tip to −; (D) both wires from the same + terminal to the bulb. In which does the bulb glow? Explain what is wrong with the others.
items.prompt_hi: Chaar set-up dekho: (A) sirf ek taar + se bulb ke tip tak; (B) cell ke dono taar sirf bulb ke tip ko chhoote hain; (C) ek taar + se bulb ki side tak, doosra bulb ke tip se − tak; (D) dono taar ek hi + terminal se bulb tak. Kismein bulb jalega? Baaki mein kya galat hai, batao.
items.answer: Only C. A: the loop is not complete. B: both wires touch one bulb terminal, so current does not pass through the filament. D: both wires come from the same cell terminal, so there is no loop through the cell.
hints: Ask them to trace each path with a finger from + to −
Point to whether the path goes through both bulb terminals
Prompt: only the set-up where the path goes + to bulb to ___ works
Assert: only C makes a complete loop through the filament

verified.solverAnswer: Only C glows: + to bulb side, tip to -, making a complete loop through the filament. A has one wire only, B both touch same terminal (tip), D both from + so no return to -.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your younger brother why the bulb glows only when the loop is complete, and why the bulb does not 'eat up' the electricity.
items.prompt_hi: Apne chhote bhai ko samjhao ki bulb tabhi kyon jalta hai jab loop poora ho, aur bulb bijli ko 'kha' kyon nahi jaata.
items.answer: Current can flow only around a complete loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other; a gap anywhere stops it everywhere. The same current comes out of the bulb as goes in; what gets used up is the cell's stored energy, which the bulb turns into light and heat.
hints: Invite them to start with the loop
Point to the rope or dots model
Prompt: a gap anywhere stops the current ___; the cell's ___ gets used, not the current
Assert: closed loop needed; current is not used up, the cell's energy is

verified.solverAnswer: Current needs a complete closed loop; any gap stops it. Current isn't used up; the cell's energy is converted to light and heat.

items.prompt_en: From last time: what is a closed circuit?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: closed circuit kya hota hai?
items.answer: A complete, unbroken path from one terminal of the cell, through the device, back to the other terminal, so current can flow.
hints: Ask what the word 'closed' tells you about the path
Point to the loop with no gaps
Prompt: a closed circuit is a ___ path from one terminal back to the ___
Assert: a closed circuit is a complete loop through which current flows

verified.solverAnswer: A complete, unbroken loop path from one cell terminal through the components back to the other, so current flows.
