skills.title: Name common non-metals (oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, sulphur, chlorine, iodine, hydrogen, helium, phosphorus) and say whether each is a solid, liquid or gas
Explain why oxygen, carbon and nitrogen are essential to living things
Connect non-metals to everyday uses: graphite pencils, chlorine in water, iodised salt, nitrogen in chips packets, fertilisers, rocket fuel, balloons

expectations: Non-metals can be solids (carbon, sulphur, iodine, phosphorus), a liquid (bromine) or gases (oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, chlorine, helium).
Oxygen is needed by living things to release energy from food (respiration) and for burning; hospitals give oxygen to patients who cannot get enough from air.
Carbon is part of all living things (our food, our bodies, wood); graphite in pencils and diamond are forms of carbon, and coal is mostly carbon used as fuel.

Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air; plants need nitrogen compounds from the soil to make proteins, which is why fertilisers contain nitrogen; nitrogen gas is filled in chips packets to keep them fresh.

Other uses: chlorine kills germs in drinking water; iodine is used in antiseptics and in iodised salt; sulphur in medicines and to toughen rubber; hydrogen and oxygen as rocket fuel; helium in balloons.

misconceptions.belief: Non-metals are not useful; metals do all the important jobs.
signs: Says 'we only need metals'
Cannot name a single use of a non-metal

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement about non-metals is true?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Non-metals ke baare mein kaunsi baat sahi hai?

options.text: Non-metals are mostly useless; metals do all the important work
Our bodies, the air we breathe and our food are built mostly from non-metals like oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen
Non-metals are only used to make poisons

remediation.representation: A 'remove it' thought experiment card: picture the world with each non-metal taken away (no oxygen, no carbon in food)
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child what would stop first in each case and build a use-list from their answers

misconceptions.belief: All non-metals are gases.
signs: Says sulphur or carbon must be a metal because they are solids
Lists only gases when asked for non-metals

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which of these is a non-metal that is a solid?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inmein se kaunsa non-metal thos (solid) hai?

options.text: None; all non-metals are gases
Sulphur, the yellow powder
Oxygen

remediation.representation: A three-column state chart (solid, liquid, gas) with non-metal cards to sort
remediation.moveShape: Have the child place carbon, sulphur and iodine, then bromine, then the gases, and notice all three columns fill

misconceptions.belief: The air is mostly oxygen.
signs: Guesses that air is 'about 80% oxygen'
Has never heard that most of the air is nitrogen

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which gas makes up most of the air around us?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hamare aas-paas ki hawa ka sabse bada hissa kaunsi gas hai?

options.text: Oxygen
Nitrogen, about 78 out of every 100 parts
Carbon dioxide

remediation.representation: A 100-bead jar: 78 blue (nitrogen), 21 red (oxygen), 1 white (other gases)
remediation.moveShape: Let the child guess the split first, then count the beads into the jar

items.prompt_en: Name two non-metals that are gases and one that is a solid.
items.prompt_hi: Do aise non-metals batao jo gas hain aur ek jo solid hai.
items.answer: Gases: for example oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, chlorine or helium. Solid: for example carbon, sulphur, iodine or phosphorus.
hints: Ask which gas we breathe in
Point to pencil lead as a solid non-metal
Prompt: oxygen and ___ are gases; ___ is a solid
Assert: oxygen and nitrogen are gases; carbon is a solid non-metal

verified.solverAnswer: Gases: oxygen, nitrogen (also hydrogen, chlorine). Solid: carbon (or sulphur, phosphorus, iodine).

items.prompt_en: Pencil 'lead' is not the metal lead at all. Which non-metal is it really made of?
items.prompt_hi: Pencil ki 'lead' asal mein lead dhaatu nahi hai. Ye asal mein kis non-metal se bani hoti hai?
items.answer: Graphite, a form of carbon (mixed with clay).
hints: Ask what leaves the grey mark on paper
Point to graphite as a form of carbon
Prompt: pencil lead is ___, a form of ___
Assert: pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon

verified.solverAnswer: Graphite, a form of carbon.
verified.note: HINT LEAK: hint 2 ('Point to graphite as a form of carbon') states the answer outright.

items.prompt_en: Predict: if you open a packet of chips and leave the chips in an open bowl for two days, will they stay crisp and fresh-tasting? Then think: why are unopened packets filled with nitrogen gas instead of air?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar chips ka packet khol ke chips ko khuli katori mein do din chhod do, toh kya wo kurkure aur taaze rahenge? Phir socho: band packets mein hawa ki jagah nitrogen gas kyon bhari jaati hai?
items.answer: They go soft by taking in moisture from the air, and can taste stale because oxygen reacts with the oil in them. Nitrogen does not react with the chips, so filling the packet with it keeps out oxygen and moisture and also cushions the chips.
hints: Ask for a guess about crispness and taste
Point to oxygen and moisture in the open air
Prompt: nitrogen keeps ___ and moisture away from the chips
Assert: open chips go soft and stale; nitrogen keeps them fresh

verified.solverAnswer: No, chips go soft/stale as they absorb moisture and react with oxygen; nitrogen is unreactive so it keeps chips fresh and cushions them.

items.prompt_en: Predict: if air were divided into 100 equal parts, about how many parts would be oxygen, and how many would be nitrogen?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar hawa ko 100 barabar hisson mein baanta jaaye, toh lagbhag kitne hisse oxygen honge aur kitne nitrogen?
items.answer: About 21 parts oxygen and about 78 parts nitrogen; the last 1 part is other gases such as argon and carbon dioxide.
hints: Ask for their guess before any numbers are given
Point to nitrogen being the bigger part
Prompt: about ___ parts nitrogen and ___ parts oxygen
Assert: about 78 nitrogen, 21 oxygen, 1 other gases

verified.solverAnswer: About 78 parts nitrogen and 21 parts oxygen.

items.prompt_en: Why does a farmer add fertiliser containing nitrogen to the soil, even though the air is full of nitrogen gas?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa mein itni saari nitrogen gas hone ke baawajood kisaan mitti mein nitrogen wala khaad kyon daalta hai?
items.answer: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas from the air directly; they take in nitrogen compounds from the soil through their roots to make proteins. Fertilisers, and bacteria in the root nodules of pulse crops, supply these.
acceptable: paudhe hawa ki nitrogen seedhe nahi le sakte
hints: Ask how a plant takes in nutrients
Point to roots in the soil, not leaves in the air
Prompt: plants take nitrogen ___ from the soil, not nitrogen ___ from the air
Assert: plants need nitrogen compounds from soil to make proteins

verified.solverAnswer: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; they take nitrogen compounds (nitrates) via roots to make proteins; fertiliser supplies these.

items.prompt_en: Why is chlorine (or bleaching powder, which releases it) added to water in city water tanks?
items.prompt_hi: Shehar ki paani ki tankiyon mein chlorine (ya bleaching powder, jisse chlorine nikalti hai) kyon daali jaati hai?
items.answer: To kill germs in the water so that it is safe to drink.
hints: Ask what might be living in untreated water
Point to chlorine as a germ-killer
Prompt: chlorine ___ germs so water is safe to ___
Assert: chlorine kills germs in drinking water

verified.solverAnswer: Chlorine kills germs/disinfects, making drinking water safe.

items.prompt_en: Compare oxygen and nitrogen, the two main gases in air. Which one do we need for breathing and burning, and what job does the other do for plants?
items.prompt_hi: Hawa ki do mukhya gases, oxygen aur nitrogen, ki tulna karo. Saans lene aur jalne ke liye kaunsi chahiye, aur doosri gas paudhon ke liye kya kaam karti hai?
items.answer: Oxygen is needed for breathing (respiration) and for burning; nitrogen, in the form of nitrogen compounds in the soil, helps plants make proteins and grow.
acceptable: oxygen for breathing, nitrogen for plant proteins
hints: Ask which gas a hospital cylinder holds
Point to nitrogen in fertilisers
Prompt: ___ for breathing and burning; ___ for plant proteins
Assert: oxygen for breathing and burning; nitrogen for plant proteins

verified.solverAnswer: Oxygen for breathing and burning; nitrogen helps plants make proteins (via nitrogen compounds/fertilisers) and dilutes oxygen.

items.prompt_en: Why does the packet of salt in your kitchen say 'iodised'?
items.prompt_hi: Tumhare kitchen ke namak ke packet pe 'iodised' kyon likha hota hai?
items.answer: A small amount of an iodine compound is added because our body needs a little iodine; too little iodine can cause goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.
hints: Ask what non-metal name is hidden in 'iodised'
Point to the thyroid gland in the neck
Prompt: a little ___ is added to prevent ___
Assert: iodised salt gives the body iodine and prevents goitre

verified.solverAnswer: Iodine is added to prevent iodine deficiency/goitre (thyroid problem).

items.prompt_en: ISRO's powerful cryogenic rocket engines burn liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. What do you think comes out of the exhaust, and why is hydrogen a good fuel?
items.prompt_hi: ISRO ke shaktishali cryogenic rocket engine liquid hydrogen ko liquid oxygen ke saath jalaate hain. Socho, exhaust se kya nikalta hoga, aur hydrogen accha fuel kyon hai?
items.answer: Mostly water vapour, because hydrogen combines with oxygen to form water; hydrogen gives out a very large amount of energy for its weight.
hints: Ask what is made when hydrogen and oxygen join
Point to H and O in water
Prompt: hydrogen + oxygen makes ___
Assert: the exhaust is water vapour; hydrogen packs a lot of energy

verified.solverAnswer: Water vapour; hydrogen releases a lot of energy and its burning gives clean exhaust.

items.prompt_en: Aman says, 'Non-metals are useless; we should only study metals.' Give him three examples that prove him wrong.
items.prompt_hi: Aman kehta hai, 'Non-metals bekaar hain, hume sirf metals padhne chahiye.' Use galat saabit karne ke liye teen examples do.
items.answer: For example: oxygen for breathing and hospitals; carbon in all food and in pencil lead; nitrogen in fertilisers and chips packets; chlorine to make drinking water safe; iodine in iodised salt.
hints: Ask what we breathe every second
Point to food, pencils and drinking water
Prompt: ___ for breathing, ___ in food, ___ in fertilisers
Assert: oxygen, carbon and nitrogen alone show non-metals are essential

verified.solverAnswer: Oxygen for breathing; carbon in food/fuel/pencils; nitrogen in fertilisers/proteins; also chlorine, iodine, sulphur.

items.prompt_en: Draw a 'non-metal map' of your body and home: label one place where you find oxygen, carbon, nitrogen and chlorine or iodine.
items.prompt_hi: Apne shareer aur ghar ka ek 'non-metal map' banao: oxygen, carbon, nitrogen aur chlorine ya iodine kahaan milte hain, har ek ki ek jagah label karo.
items.answer: Oxygen: in the air you breathe or a hospital cylinder. Carbon: in food, wood, a pencil or coal. Nitrogen: in air, a chips packet or fertiliser. Chlorine: in treated tap water. Iodine: in iodised salt or an antiseptic.
hints: Invite them to draw themselves and a kitchen first
Point to the air, the food and the salt box
Prompt: oxygen in the ___, carbon in ___, iodine in ___
Assert: non-metals are everywhere in the body and the home

verified.solverAnswer: Oxygen in air/lungs/water; carbon in food/pencil/body; nitrogen in air/proteins; iodine in salt or chlorine in drinking water.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your friend why life on Earth would be impossible without non-metals.
items.prompt_hi: Apne dost ko samjhao ki non-metals ke bina dharti pe jeevan kyon sambhav nahi hota.
items.answer: Living things are built mainly from non-metals such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen; we need oxygen to release energy from food, plants need nitrogen to make proteins, and water itself is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
hints: Invite them to start with what our bodies are made of
Point to breathing, food and water
Prompt: our bodies are built from ___, and we need ___ to breathe
Assert: living things are made of and depend on non-metals

verified.solverAnswer: Bodies, food, air, water are made from/depend on non-metals (C, H, O, N); we need oxygen to breathe and carbon-based food.

items.prompt_en: From last time: name the yellow non-metal powder used in some medicines and to make rubber stronger.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: wo peela non-metal powder kaunsa hai jo kuch dawaiyon mein aur rubber ko mazboot banane mein use hota hai?
items.answer: Sulphur.
hints: Ask what colour the powder is
Point to the word 'gandhak'
Prompt: the yellow non-metal is ___
Assert: it is sulphur, a solid non-metal

verified.solverAnswer: Sulphur.

workedExample.problem: Explain why a patient in hospital may be given oxygen from a cylinder.
steps: Every cell in the body needs oxygen to release energy from food (respiration)
Air has about 21% oxygen, enough for a healthy person
A patient with weak or damaged lungs cannot take in enough oxygen from ordinary air
The cylinder supplies air with much more oxygen through a mask or tube
More oxygen reaches the blood and the cells, helping the patient breathe and recover
fadedVersion: Every cell needs ___ to release energy from food
Air has about ___% oxygen, enough for a healthy person
A patient with weak ___ cannot take in enough oxygen
The cylinder supplies much more ___ through a mask
More oxygen reaches the ___ and the cells

skills.title: Define a physical change (no new substance; only shape, size or state changes) and give examples
Define a chemical change (a new substance with new properties forms) and recognise its signs: gas, colour change, heat or light, new smell, new solid
Classify everyday changes using evidence, knowing that 'can it be reversed?' is a clue but not the rule
Tell melting apart from dissolving and know that dissolved substances are still present

expectations: In a physical change, a substance changes its shape, size or state (solid, liquid, gas) but no new substance is formed; for example melting ghee, freezing water, tearing paper and dissolving sugar.
In a chemical change, one or more new substances with different properties are formed; for example burning a wick, curdling milk, cooking an egg, rusting and fruit ripening.
Signs of a chemical change include gas bubbles, a change of colour, heat or light given out, a new smell, or a new solid forming.

Many physical changes are easy to reverse (melting, freezing), but some are not (tearing paper, breaking glass); most chemical changes cannot be reversed easily. So reversibility is a clue, not the rule; the real test is whether a new substance forms.

Melting is a solid turning into a liquid when heated; dissolving is a substance spreading into a liquid to form a solution. Both are physical changes, and a dissolved substance is still there and still has mass.

misconceptions.belief: All changes can be reversed.
signs: Says curd can be turned back into milk
Thinks a cooked egg can become raw again if cooled

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which change can NOT be reversed to get the original substance back?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsa badlav ulta karke original cheez waapas nahi la sakte?

options.text: None; every change can be undone
Making curd from milk
Melting butter

remediation.representation: Before-and-after card pairs (milk to curd, ice to water, raw to cooked egg) with an 'undo' button that works only on some
remediation.moveShape: Let the child press undo on each and explain why it fails for curd and the egg

misconceptions.belief: Melting ice is a chemical change because it looks different.
signs: Calls any change of appearance 'chemical'
Says water is a different substance from ice

diagnostic.prompt_en: Ice melts into water. Has a new substance been formed?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Barf pighal ke paani ban jaati hai. Kya koi nayi cheez bani?

options.text: Yes, water is a different substance from ice, so it is a chemical change
No, it is the same substance in a different state, so it is a physical change
Yes, because it feels cold

remediation.representation: A particle view: the same water particles packed in ice, then sliding past each other in liquid
remediation.moveShape: Freeze the melted water again in the animation and ask whether anything new appeared

misconceptions.belief: When sugar or salt is stirred into water, it melts.
signs: Uses 'melt' for sugar in chai
Thinks dissolving needs heat like melting

diagnostic.prompt_en: When sugar is stirred into water and seems to disappear, what has happened to it?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Jab cheeni ko paani mein hilaate hain aur wo gayab si ho jaati hai, toh uske saath kya hua?

options.text: The sugar melted
The sugar dissolved; it is still there, spread through the water, which is why the water tastes sweet
The sugar was destroyed

remediation.representation: Two-panel contrast: ghee melting in a warm pan with no water, sugar dissolving in cold water
remediation.moveShape: Ask which panel needs heat and which needs a liquid; name each one

misconceptions.belief: A dissolved substance has disappeared and no longer has any mass.
signs: Predicts no change in weight after dissolving sugar
Says the salt in salty water is 'gone'

diagnostic.prompt_en: A glass of water weighs 200 g. Twenty grams of sugar is completely dissolved in it. What does it weigh now?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Paani ke ek glass ka wazan 200 g hai. Usme 20 g cheeni poori tarah ghol di gayi. Ab uska wazan kitna hoga?

options.text: 200 g, because dissolved sugar weighs nothing
220 g, because the sugar is still there
Less than 200 g

remediation.representation: Kitchen-scale animation with the reading staying at 220 g as the sugar crystals vanish from view
remediation.moveShape: Have the child predict the reading before stirring, then evaporate a drop to show sugar left behind

items.prompt_en: Is melting ghee a physical or a chemical change? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Ghee ka pighalna physical badlav hai ya chemical? Kyon?
items.answer: Physical: it is still ghee, only changed from solid to liquid, and it becomes solid again when it cools.
hints: Ask what happens to melted ghee kept in a cool place
Point to no new substance appearing
Prompt: it is still ___, only its ___ changed
Assert: melting ghee is physical; it is still ghee

verified.solverAnswer: Physical change; it is still ghee, only the state changed from solid to liquid, reversible by cooling.

items.prompt_en: Give two signs that tell you a chemical change has happened.
items.prompt_hi: Do aise sanket batao jinse pata chale ki chemical badlav hua hai.
items.answer: Any two of: gas bubbles, a change of colour, heat or light given out, a new smell, a new solid forming.
hints: Ask what they notice when food is cooked
Point to bubbles, colour and smell
Prompt: a chemical change can give ___ bubbles or a new ___
Assert: gas, colour change, heat or light, new smell or new solid

verified.solverAnswer: Gas bubbles/fizzing, colour change, heat or light given out, new smell, new solid (precipitate).

items.prompt_en: Put half a spoon of baking soda into a cup and add a few spoons of lemon juice or vinegar. Predict: what will you see and hear? Will it be a physical or a chemical change?
items.prompt_hi: Ek cup mein aadha chammach baking soda daalo aur usme kuch chammach nimbu ka ras ya sirka daalo. Guess karo: kya dikhega aur kya sunaayi dega? Ye physical badlav hoga ya chemical?
items.answer: It fizzes and bubbles with a hissing sound as carbon dioxide gas forms; a new substance (the gas) is made, so it is a chemical change.
hints: Ask for a guess before mixing
Point to the bubbles as a new gas
Prompt: the bubbles are a new ___, so it is a ___ change
Assert: fizzing with carbon dioxide gas; a chemical change

verified.solverAnswer: Fizzing and hissing/bubbles of carbon dioxide; chemical change.

items.prompt_en: Weigh a glass of water on a kitchen scale, then stir in two spoons of sugar until you cannot see it. Predict: will the weight go up, stay the same or go down?
items.prompt_hi: Kitchen ke taraazu pe paani ka glass tolo, phir do chammach cheeni ghol do jab tak dikhe nahi. Guess karo: wazan badhega, utna hi rahega ya ghatega?
items.answer: It goes up by the weight of the sugar; the sugar has dissolved but it is still in the water.
hints: Ask for a guess before stirring
Point to the sweet taste as proof the sugar is still there
Prompt: dissolved sugar is still ___, so the weight ___
Assert: the weight rises by the sugar's weight

verified.solverAnswer: Weight goes up by the weight of sugar (sugar still present).

items.prompt_en: Ask an adult to cut an apple into two pieces. Leave one piece open on a plate and dip the other in lemon water. Predict which one turns brown faster. Is browning a physical or a chemical change?
items.prompt_hi: Kisi bade se seb ke do tukde katwao. Ek tukda plate pe khula chhod do aur doosre ko nimbu-paani mein dubo do. Guess karo kaunsa jaldi bhoora hoga. Bhoora hona physical badlav hai ya chemical?
items.answer: The open piece turns brown faster. Browning is a chemical change: substances in the apple react with oxygen in the air to make new brown substances; lemon juice slows this.
hints: Ask what the open piece is touching
Point to the colour change as a sign
Prompt: the cut apple reacts with ___ to form new ___ substances
Assert: the open piece browns first; browning is a chemical change

verified.solverAnswer: The open piece browns faster; chemical change (reaction with oxygen); lemon slows it.

items.prompt_en: Tearing a sheet of paper cannot be undone, yet it is a physical change. Why?
items.prompt_hi: Kaagaz phaadna ulta nahi kiya ja sakta, phir bhi ye physical badlav hai. Kyon?
items.answer: No new substance is formed: the torn pieces are still paper. Whether a change can be reversed is only a clue; the real test is whether a new substance forms.
hints: Ask what the torn pieces are made of
Point to the test of a new substance
Prompt: the pieces are still ___, so no new ___ formed
Assert: still paper, so physical, even though it cannot be undone

verified.solverAnswer: Pieces are still paper; no new substance formed; so physical although not reversible.

items.prompt_en: Compare the melting of a candle's wax with the burning of its wick. Which is physical and which is chemical? Give evidence for each.
items.prompt_hi: Mombatti ke wax ke pighalne aur uski baati ke jalne ki tulna karo. Kaunsa physical hai aur kaunsa chemical? Dono ke liye saboot do.
items.answer: Melting wax is physical: the liquid wax cools back into solid wax. Burning is chemical: heat and light are given out, and new substances such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and soot form.
hints: Ask what the melted wax becomes when it drips and cools
Point to light, heat and smoke from burning
Prompt: melting wax is ___; burning gives ___ and new ___
Assert: melting is physical; burning makes new substances, so it is chemical

verified.solverAnswer: Melting wax is physical (solid to liquid, same wax, solidifies again); burning wick is chemical (heat, light, smoke, ash, new substances).

items.prompt_en: Milk left out on a hot day turns sour and forms lumps. Is this a physical or a chemical change? What is your evidence?
items.prompt_hi: Garmi ke din bahar chhoda doodh khatta ho ke phat jaata hai. Ye physical badlav hai ya chemical? Tumhara saboot kya hai?
items.answer: Chemical: there is a new sour smell and taste and lumps form, and it cannot be turned back into fresh milk.
hints: Ask how sour milk smells compared with fresh milk
Point to the lumps as a new solid
Prompt: new ___ and lumps show a ___ change
Assert: souring and curdling is chemical

verified.solverAnswer: Chemical change; sour smell/taste, lumps form: new substances, can't get fresh milk back.

items.prompt_en: Think of a festival kitchen while sweets are being made. Name one physical change and one chemical change that happen there.
items.prompt_hi: Socho tyohaar ke din kitchen mein mithai ban rahi hai. Wahaan hone wala ek physical badlav aur ek chemical badlav batao.
items.answer: Physical: sugar dissolving in water for the syrup, ghee melting, dough being rolled. Chemical: dough or besan turning golden-brown when fried or roasted, or milk being made into chenna or paneer with lemon juice.
hints: Ask what happens to sugar in water and to besan in hot ghee
Point to colour and smell changes during frying
Prompt: ___ dissolving is physical; ___ turning golden is chemical
Assert: dissolving and melting are physical; browning when frying is chemical

verified.solverAnswer: Physical: sugar dissolving or butter/ghee melting. Chemical: frying besan turning golden brown / milk turning to khoya browning / burning.

items.prompt_en: Kunal says, 'When I stir salt into water, the salt melts.' Which word should he use, and how is it different from melting?
items.prompt_hi: Kunal kehta hai, 'Jab main namak paani mein hilaata hoon, toh namak pighal jaata hai.' Use kaunsa shabd use karna chahiye, aur wo pighalne se alag kaise hai?
items.answer: Dissolves. Dissolving is the salt spreading into the water to form a solution; melting is a solid turning into a liquid by heating, and salt needs a temperature of about 800 °C to melt.
hints: Ask whether any heat was used
Point to the salt spreading into the water
Prompt: salt ___ in water; melting needs ___
Assert: salt dissolves; melting needs heat and no water

verified.solverAnswer: Salt dissolves in water; melting is solid becoming liquid by heat; dissolving is mixing into a liquid and salt can be recovered by evaporating.

items.prompt_en: Sort these into a two-circle chart, 'physical' and 'chemical': freezing water into ice, cooking rice, folding a paper boat, a banana ripening, dissolving salt, toasting bread, blowing up a balloon.
items.prompt_hi: Inhe do gole wale chart mein baanto, 'physical' aur 'chemical': paani ka barf banna, chawal pakaana, kaagaz ki naav banana, kele ka pakna, namak gholna, bread toast karna, gubbara phulaana.
items.answer: Physical: freezing water, folding a paper boat, dissolving salt, blowing up a balloon. Chemical: cooking rice, a banana ripening, toasting bread.
hints: Invite them to ask 'is there a new substance?' for each
Point to colour and smell changes in cooking and ripening
Prompt: the ones with a new substance go in the ___ circle
Assert: freezing, folding, dissolving and inflating are physical; cooking, ripening and toasting are chemical

verified.solverAnswer: Physical: freezing water, folding paper boat, dissolving salt, blowing up balloon. Chemical: cooking rice, banana ripening, toasting bread.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger child how to tell a physical change from a chemical change, using two examples from the kitchen.
items.prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko kitchen ke do examples se samjhao ki physical aur chemical badlav mein farak kaise pehchaanein.
items.answer: Ask: has a new substance formed? If not, it is physical, like ice melting or sugar dissolving. If yes, with signs like a new colour, smell, gas, heat or light, it is chemical, like a roti browning or milk turning into curd.
hints: Invite them to start with the key question
Point to one example of each in the kitchen
Prompt: no new substance means ___; a new substance means ___
Assert: new substance decides; melting is physical, curd-making is chemical

verified.solverAnswer: Ask: is a new substance formed? Melting butter is physical (same butter); making curd from milk or cooking roti is chemical.

items.prompt_en: From last time: when water freezes in the freezer, is it a physical or a chemical change?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: jab freezer mein paani jamta hai, toh ye physical badlav hai ya chemical?
items.answer: Physical: it is still water, only in the solid state.
hints: Ask what the ice becomes when it melts
Point to it being the same substance
Prompt: freezing changes only the ___
Assert: freezing is a physical change

verified.solverAnswer: Physical change.

workedExample.problem: Is roasting a chapati on a tawa a physical or a chemical change? Decide with evidence.
steps: List what you observe: brown spots appear, the smell changes, and the chapati becomes firmer and puffs up
Check for signs of a chemical change: there is a colour change and a new smell
Ask: can you get the raw dough back? No
So new substances have formed while the dough was heated
Roasting the chapati is a chemical change (kneading and rolling the dough were physical changes)
fadedVersion: List what you observe: brown ___ appear and the ___ changes
Check for signs: there is a ___ change and a new smell
Ask: can you get the raw ___ back? No
So new ___ have formed while it was heated
Roasting is a ___ change; rolling the dough was ___

skills.title: Describe combustion as a chemical change in which a fuel reacts with oxygen, giving out heat and usually light
State the three things needed for burning (fuel, oxygen, ignition temperature) and explain how fires are put out by removing one of them
Explain rusting as a slow chemical change that needs oxygen and water, and compare it with combustion
Explain that burning does not destroy matter: it turns into gases (carbon dioxide, water vapour), smoke and ash

expectations: Combustion (burning) is a chemical change in which a substance (the fuel) reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and usually light.
Burning needs three things: fuel, oxygen (air) and enough heat to reach the ignition temperature; removing any one of them puts the fire out.
Fanning a sigri pushes more oxygen-rich air to the fuel so it burns more strongly; covering a flame cuts off oxygen and it goes out.
Burning does not destroy matter: wood, wax or oil turn into carbon dioxide, water vapour, smoke and ash, which go into the air or stay behind.
Rusting is also a chemical change that needs oxygen, and water too, but it is slow and gives no flame.

Fire safety: water cools burning wood and paper below the ignition temperature; sand, a lid or a blanket cuts off air; water must never be used on burning oil or on electrical fires; children should never play with fire.

misconceptions.belief: Burning destroys matter completely.
signs: Says the candle wax 'is gone' or 'became nothing'
Thinks the light ash shows most of the wood vanished

diagnostic.prompt_en: A candle burns for an hour and becomes much shorter. Where did most of the wax go?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek mombatti ek ghante jalti hai aur bahut chhoti ho jaati hai. Zyadatar wax kahaan gaya?

options.text: It was destroyed and is gone completely
It turned into gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour that went into the air
It all melted and dripped onto the table

remediation.representation: A closed-box balance animation: wood burns inside a sealed box and the scale reading does not change
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to list everything that came out of the fire, including invisible gases, before revealing the scale

misconceptions.belief: Fanning works by giving the fire more heat or by blowing heat into it; oxygen has nothing to do with it.
signs: Says fanning 'pushes heat' into the coals
Cannot explain why covering a flame puts it out

diagnostic.prompt_en: Why does fanning a sigri make the coals glow brighter?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Sigri ko pankha jhalne se koyle zyada tez kyon chamakne lagte hain?

options.text: Fanning pushes more oxygen-rich air to the coals
Fanning puts heat from your hand into the coals
Fanning makes no real difference

remediation.representation: Fire-triangle diagram with the oxygen side glowing brighter as an arrow of fresh air arrives
remediation.moveShape: Contrast fanning with covering using the triangle; ask which side changes each time

misconceptions.belief: Water can put out every kind of fire.
signs: Says 'just throw water' for a kadhai oil fire
Would pour water on a sparking appliance

diagnostic.prompt_en: Oil in a kadhai catches fire. What should an adult do?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kadhai ke tel mein aag lag jaati hai. Bade ko kya karna chahiye?

options.text: Throw water on it
Turn off the gas and cover the kadhai with a lid to cut off air
Fan it to blow it out

remediation.representation: Safety cartoon strip: water flung on burning oil splashing flames outward, beside a lid calmly placed on top
remediation.moveShape: Ask which side of the fire triangle the lid removes, and why water makes oil fires worse

misconceptions.belief: Rusting and burning have nothing in common; rusting is just dirt forming.
signs: Calls rusting a physical change
Does not link rust to oxygen

diagnostic.prompt_en: What do rusting and burning have in common?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Jung lagne aur jalne mein kya common hai?

options.text: Nothing; rusting is just dirt forming on iron
Both are chemical changes in which a substance combines with oxygen
Both always need a flame

remediation.representation: Fast and slow timeline: a matchstick burning in seconds and a nail rusting over weeks, both with an oxygen label
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child what each one takes from the air and what new substance each makes

items.prompt_en: Which gas from the air is needed for burning?
items.prompt_hi: Jalne ke liye hawa ki kaunsi gas zaroori hai?
items.answer: Oxygen.
hints: Ask which gas we also breathe for energy
Point to the gas that a covered flame runs out of
Prompt: burning needs the gas ___
Assert: oxygen is needed for burning

verified.solverAnswer: Oxygen.

items.prompt_en: Name the three things needed for a fire to burn.
items.prompt_hi: Aag jalne ke liye teen zaroori cheezein batao.
items.answer: Fuel, oxygen (air) and enough heat to reach the ignition temperature.
hints: Ask what is burning, what it needs from the air, and what starts it
Point to the three sides of the fire triangle
Prompt: fuel, ___ and ___
Assert: fuel, oxygen and heat make the fire triangle

verified.solverAnswer: Fuel, oxygen (air) and heat (ignition temperature).

items.prompt_en: Think-only question; never try this yourself. In class, your teacher lights two identical candles and covers one with a small glass jar and the other with a big glass jar. Predict which flame goes out first, and why.
items.prompt_hi: Sirf sochne wala sawaal hai, ise khud kabhi try mat karna. Class mein teacher do ek jaisi mombattiyan jalaate hain aur ek ko chhote kaanch ke jar se aur doosri ko bade jar se dhak dete hain. Guess karo kaunsi lau pehle bujhegi, aur kyon?
items.answer: The one under the small jar goes out first, because it has less air, so its oxygen gets used up sooner.
hints: Ask which jar holds more air
Point to oxygen being used up as it burns
Prompt: the small jar has less ___, so it runs out ___
Assert: the small jar's flame dies first; its oxygen runs out sooner

verified.solverAnswer: The candle under the small jar goes out first; less oxygen available.

items.prompt_en: Think-only question. A piece of wood is burnt completely inside a strong sealed box from which nothing can escape, and the whole box is weighed before and after. Predict: will the total mass go down, stay the same or go up?
items.prompt_hi: Sirf sochne wala sawaal. Lakdi ka ek tukda ek mazboot band dibbe mein poora jala diya jaata hai jahaan se kuch bhi bahar nahi nikal sakta, aur poore dibbe ko pehle aur baad mein tola jaata hai. Guess karo: kul wazan ghatega, utna hi rahega ya badhega?
items.answer: It stays the same: the wood and the oxygen it used turn into ash, smoke and gases that are all still inside the box; nothing is destroyed. In an open fire the gases escape, which is why the ash left behind is lighter.
hints: Ask for a guess before discussing
Point to the gases being trapped inside the box
Prompt: the matter changes into ash and ___, but none of it is ___
Assert: the total mass stays the same; burning changes matter, it does not destroy it

verified.solverAnswer: Stays the same; no matter lost, burning converts it to ash and gases all trapped in box.

items.prompt_en: Think-only question. In a science video, a paper cup full of water is held over a steady flame. Predict: will the paper cup catch fire before the water boils?
items.prompt_hi: Sirf sochne wala sawaal. Ek science video mein paani se bhara kaagaz ka cup ek sthir lau ke upar pakda jaata hai. Guess karo: kya paani ubalne se pehle kaagaz ka cup jal jaayega?
items.answer: No. The water keeps taking heat away from the paper, so the paper stays below its ignition temperature while there is water in it.
hints: Ask where the flame's heat goes
Point to the water soaking up the heat
Prompt: the water keeps the paper below its ___ temperature
Assert: the cup does not burn while it holds water

verified.solverAnswer: No, cup doesn't catch fire before water boils; the water absorbs heat and keeps paper below its ignition temperature.

items.prompt_en: Why does fanning a sigri or a chulha make it burn more strongly?
items.prompt_hi: Sigri ya chulhe ko pankha jhalne se wo zyada tez kyon jalta hai?
items.answer: Fanning pushes more fresh, oxygen-rich air to the fuel, so it burns faster and gives more heat and light.
hints: Ask what the moving air carries
Point to the oxygen side of the fire triangle
Prompt: fanning brings more ___ to the fuel
Assert: fanning supplies more oxygen, so the fire burns stronger

verified.solverAnswer: Fanning supplies more oxygen (air) to the fire so it burns faster/brighter.

items.prompt_en: Why must water never be thrown on burning oil in a kadhai, or on an electrical fire?
items.prompt_hi: Kadhai ke jalte tel pe ya bijli ki aag pe kabhi paani kyon nahi daalna chahiye?
items.answer: Oil floats on water and the water turns to steam explosively, splashing burning oil and spreading the fire; water also conducts electricity and could give a shock. Adults should turn off the gas or power and cover the fire to cut off air.
hints: Ask what oil does when it meets water
Point to water conducting electricity
Prompt: water spreads an oil fire and ___ electricity
Assert: water makes oil fires spread and electrical fires deadly; cover and cut off instead

verified.solverAnswer: Water is denser than oil, sinks and boils, splashing burning oil; spreads fire; water conducts electricity causing shock. Use lid/sand/CO2 extinguisher and switch off power.

items.prompt_en: Compare the rusting of an iron nail with the burning of a matchstick. Give one way they are the same and two ways they are different.
items.prompt_hi: Lohe ki keel ke jung lagne aur maachis ki teeli ke jalne ki tulna karo. Ek samaanta aur do farak batao.
items.answer: Same: both are chemical changes in which a substance combines with oxygen. Different: rusting is slow (days to weeks) and needs water, with no flame or light; burning is fast and gives out heat and light.
hints: Ask what both take from the air
Point to speed and to flame
Prompt: both use ___; rusting is ___ and burning is ___
Assert: both combine with oxygen; rusting is slow without flame, burning is fast with heat and light

verified.solverAnswer: Same: both chemical changes combining with oxygen. Different: rusting slow, no flame/light/heat noticeable; burning fast with heat and light. Rust is new solid, burning produces gases.

items.prompt_en: Why do petrol pumps keep buckets of sand, and why do firefighters cover some fires with foam?
items.prompt_hi: Petrol pump pe ret ki baaltiyan kyon rakhi jaati hain, aur fire-fighters kuch aag ko foam se kyon dhakte hain?
items.answer: Sand and foam cover the burning fuel and cut off its oxygen, so the fire goes out; water is not safe on burning petrol because petrol floats on water.
hints: Ask which side of the fire triangle the sand removes
Point to petrol floating on water
Prompt: sand and foam cut off the ___
Assert: sand and foam smother the fire by cutting off oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Sand and foam cover/smother the fire, cutting off oxygen (and cool), and water would spread petrol fires.

items.prompt_en: In some states, farmers burn leftover crop straw (parali) in the fields. Using what you know about combustion, explain where the straw's matter goes and why cities far away get smoky air.
items.prompt_hi: Kuch rajyon mein kisaan khet mein bachi parali jalaate hain. Combustion ke baare mein jo jaante ho uske hisaab se samjhao ki parali ka padarth kahaan jaata hai aur door ke shehron ki hawa dhuaan-dhuaan kyon ho jaati hai.
items.answer: Burning turns the straw into carbon dioxide, water vapour, smoke particles and ash; the gases and smoke rise into the air and winds carry them to cities, where the smoke pollutes the air.
hints: Ask what you can see rising from a burning field
Point to wind direction towards cities
Prompt: the straw becomes ___, smoke and ash, and the ___ carries the smoke
Assert: the straw's matter becomes gases and smoke that winds carry to cities

verified.solverAnswer: Straw burns to carbon dioxide, water vapour, smoke and ash (particles); wind carries smoke and particles far to cities, causing smog.

items.prompt_en: Pinky says, 'After a bonfire, the ash is so light, so most of the wood was destroyed into nothing.' What is the mistake?
items.prompt_hi: Pinky kehti hai, 'Alaav ke baad raakh itni halki hoti hai, matlab zyadatar lakdi khatam ho ke kuch nahi bachi.' Galti kya hai?
items.answer: The wood's matter was not destroyed; most of it turned into gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour) and smoke that went into the air. Only a small part was left as ash.
hints: Ask what rises from a fire besides flames
Point to invisible gases
Prompt: most of the wood became ___ that went into the air
Assert: nothing was destroyed; most of the wood became gases and smoke

verified.solverAnswer: Matter isn't destroyed; most of the wood became gases (carbon dioxide, water vapour) and smoke in the air; ash is only the leftover solid.

items.prompt_en: Draw a fire triangle and label its three sides. Next to each side, draw one way of removing it to put a fire out.
items.prompt_hi: Ek fire triangle banao aur uski teeno bhujaon pe label lagao. Har bhuja ke paas aag bujhaane ke liye use hataane ka ek tareeka banao.
items.answer: Fuel: remove the fuel, for example turn off the gas. Oxygen: cut off air with a lid, sand or a fire blanket. Heat: cool it with water (only for wood, paper or cloth fires).
hints: Invite them to draw and label the triangle first
Point to one side at a time
Prompt: turn off the ___, cover to cut off ___, cool with ___
Assert: remove fuel, oxygen or heat and the fire goes out

verified.solverAnswer: Triangle sides: fuel, oxygen, heat. Remove fuel (switch off gas/clear grass), cut oxygen (cover with lid/blanket/foam), remove heat (cool with water).

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger child what a fire needs to burn, why a fire goes out when it is covered, and why children must never play with fire.
items.prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko samjhao ki aag ko jalne ke liye kya chahiye, dhakne pe aag kyon bujh jaati hai, aur bachchon ko aag se kabhi kyon nahi khelna chahiye.
items.answer: A fire needs fuel, oxygen from the air and enough heat; covering it cuts off the oxygen so it goes out. Fire spreads fast and burns skin, so only adults should handle it.
hints: Invite them to start with the fire triangle
Point to covering removing the oxygen
Prompt: fire needs fuel, ___ and heat; covering cuts off the ___
Assert: fuel, oxygen and heat; covering removes oxygen; only adults handle fire

verified.solverAnswer: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat; covering cuts off oxygen so it goes out; fire is dangerous, only adults handle it.

items.prompt_en: From last time: is burning a physical or a chemical change, and what does it give out?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: jalna physical badlav hai ya chemical, aur isse kya nikalta hai?
items.answer: A chemical change; it gives out heat and light, and makes new substances such as carbon dioxide.
hints: Ask whether ash can turn back into wood
Point to heat and light from a diya
Prompt: burning is ___ and gives out ___ and ___
Assert: burning is chemical and gives out heat and light

verified.solverAnswer: Chemical change; gives out heat and light.

workedExample.problem: A sigri's coals are glowing dimly. Explain step by step why fanning makes them burn brighter.
steps: Burning needs fuel, oxygen and heat
The coals are the fuel and are already hot enough, but they are short of oxygen
Fanning pushes fresh air, which contains oxygen, onto the coals
With more oxygen, combustion is faster, giving more heat and light
If the sigri were covered instead, the oxygen would be cut off and it would slowly go out
fadedVersion: Burning needs fuel, ___ and heat
The coals are hot enough, but they are short of ___
Fanning pushes fresh ___ onto the coals
With more oxygen, combustion is ___
If covered, the oxygen is ___ and it goes out

skills.title: Explain weathering: rocks breaking down where they are because of heating and cooling, water freezing in cracks, plant roots and rainwater
Explain erosion: broken rock and soil carried away by flowing water, wind, moving ice and sea waves
Explain how slow weathering and erosion shape land (rounded pebbles, valleys, sand dunes, deltas, soil) and how cutting trees speeds up erosion

expectations: Weathering is the slow breaking down of rocks where they are, by heating and cooling, water freezing and expanding in cracks, plant roots growing in cracks, and rainwater slowly reacting with rock.
Erosion is the carrying away of broken rock and soil by flowing water, wind, moving ice (glaciers) and sea waves.
These changes are usually very slow, taking hundreds to millions of years, although floods and landslides can move a lot of soil quickly.
Pebbles in a mountain stream become rounded because they knock and rub against each other and the riverbed as the water carries them.
Soil forms from weathered rock mixed with humus and takes hundreds of years to form a few centimetres; tree roots and grass hold soil and protect it from erosion.

misconceptions.belief: Rocks never change.
signs: Says mountains have always looked exactly as they do now
Thinks only earthquakes can change rocks

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is true about the rocks of the Himalayas?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Himalaya ki chattanon ke baare mein kya sach hai?

options.text: They have looked exactly the same forever
They are slowly being broken down and worn away by ice, water and wind
Rocks change only in earthquakes

remediation.representation: A time-lapse slider from sharp rock to rounded pebble to sand, labelled with thousands of years
remediation.moveShape: Use the chalk-shaking experiment as a sped-up model, then ask what years of rivers would do

misconceptions.belief: Weathering and erosion are the same thing.
signs: Uses the two words interchangeably
Calls a tree root splitting a rock 'erosion'

diagnostic.prompt_en: A tree root splits a rock on a hillside. Later, rain washes the pieces down into a river. Which step is erosion?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek ped ki jad pahadi pe ek chattan ko tod deti hai. Baad mein baarish tukdon ko bahaa ke nadi mein le jaati hai. Kaunsa kadam erosion hai?

options.text: Both steps are erosion
The splitting is weathering; carrying the pieces away is erosion
The splitting is erosion; the carrying is weathering

remediation.representation: Two-stage comic: stage 1 'break it' (weathering), stage 2 'move it' (erosion)
remediation.moveShape: Give the child mixed event cards to place under 'break' or 'move'

misconceptions.belief: Land changes and soil formation happen quickly.
signs: Thinks new soil forms within a year after it is washed away
Expects a stream to round a pebble in days

diagnostic.prompt_en: How long does nature take to make a few centimetres of soil from rock?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Chattan se kuch centimetre mitti banaane mein prakriti ko kitna samay lagta hai?

options.text: A few days after rain
Hundreds of years or more
Soil was made once and never forms again

remediation.representation: A ruler next to a timeline: one centimetre of soil against a long line of centuries
remediation.moveShape: Ask how many lifetimes fit along the line before the centimetre fills

items.prompt_en: What is weathering? Give one cause of it.
items.prompt_hi: Weathering kya hai? Iska ek kaaran batao.
items.answer: Weathering is the slow breaking down of rocks where they are; causes include heating and cooling, water freezing in cracks, plant roots growing into cracks, and rainwater.
hints: Ask what could crack a rock without anyone hitting it
Point to roots and ice in cracks
Prompt: weathering is rocks breaking down ___ they are, for example by ___
Assert: weathering is rocks breaking down in place, for example by ice or roots

verified.solverAnswer: Weathering is the breaking down of rock in place into smaller pieces by water, ice, wind, temperature change, plant roots.

items.prompt_en: Name three things that can carry away broken rock and soil.
items.prompt_hi: Teen cheezein batao jo tooti chattan aur mitti ko bahaa ke le ja sakti hain.
items.answer: Any three of: flowing water (rivers and rain), wind, moving ice (glaciers), sea waves.
hints: Ask what carries sand across a desert
Point to rivers, wind and glaciers
Prompt: flowing ___, ___ and moving ___
Assert: water, wind, ice and waves cause erosion

verified.solverAnswer: Running water (rivers), wind, ice/glaciers (also waves).

items.prompt_en: Put a few small pieces of chalk, or a few sugar cubes, into a closed steel tiffin box or plastic bottle and shake it hard for three minutes. Predict what the pieces will look like and what you will find at the bottom.
items.prompt_hi: Chalk ke kuch chhote tukde, ya kuch sugar cubes, ek band steel ke tiffin ya plastic ki bottle mein daalo aur teen minute zor se hilaao. Guess karo tukde kaise dikhenge aur neeche kya milega.
items.answer: Their corners become rounded and they get smaller, and fine powder collects at the bottom, just as rocks become rounded pebbles and sand in a stream.
hints: Ask for a guess before shaking
Point to the pieces knocking into each other
Prompt: the corners become ___ and ___ collects at the bottom
Assert: rubbing rounds the pieces and makes powder, like stream pebbles

verified.solverAnswer: Pieces become rounded and smaller with chipped corners, and powder/dust collects at the bottom.

items.prompt_en: Outdoors, make two small slopes of soil in trays: one bare, one covered with grass or a layer of leaves. Pour one mug of water slowly on each from the same height. Predict which slope loses more soil.
items.prompt_hi: Bahar do tray mein mitti ki do chhoti dhalaan banao: ek khaali, ek ghaas ya patton ki parat se dhaki. Har ek pe ek hi oonchai se dheere dheere ek mug paani daalo. Guess karo kaunsi dhalaan se zyada mitti bahegi.
items.answer: The bare slope loses more soil; the grass or leaves hold the soil and slow the water down.
hints: Ask for a guess before pouring
Point to what holds the soil on the grassy slope
Prompt: plants ___ the soil and ___ the water
Assert: the bare slope erodes more; plant cover protects soil

verified.solverAnswer: The bare slope loses more soil; roots and cover protect soil and slow water.

items.prompt_en: Fill a small plastic bottle completely with water, close it tightly, put it in a plastic bag and leave it in the freezer overnight. Predict what will happen to the bottle, and how this explains cracks in rocks on cold mountains.
items.prompt_hi: Ek chhoti plastic ki bottle ko poora paani se bharo, kas ke band karo, plastic ki thaili mein rakho aur raat bhar freezer mein chhod do. Guess karo bottle ka kya hoga, aur isse thande pahadon ki chattanon mein daraar kaise samajh aati hai.
items.answer: The bottle bulges or even splits, because water expands when it freezes. In rocks, water in cracks freezes and expands, pushing the cracks wider until pieces break off.
hints: Ask for a guess before freezing
Point to ice taking more space than water
Prompt: freezing water ___ and pushes the crack ___
Assert: freezing water expands; in rock cracks it splits the rock

verified.solverAnswer: Water expands on freezing so bottle bulges/cracks/bursts; same in rock cracks, ice wedges and splits rock.

items.prompt_en: Why are the pebbles in a mountain stream round and smooth, while rocks freshly broken from a cliff are sharp?
items.prompt_hi: Pahaadi nadi ke kankar gol aur chikne kyon hote hain, jabki chattan se abhi toote tukde nukile hote hain?
items.answer: As the stream carries the pebbles, they knock and rub against each other and the riverbed for a long time, wearing away their sharp edges; fresh pieces have not been rubbed yet.
hints: Ask what happens to the pebbles as water carries them
Point to the chalk-shaking model
Prompt: rubbing and knocking wear away the ___ edges
Assert: long rubbing in the stream rounds the pebbles

verified.solverAnswer: Stream pebbles are rubbed and knocked by water and other stones for a long time, wearing sharp edges; fresh broken rocks haven't been worn yet.

items.prompt_en: Compare: (A) in Rajasthan, hot days and cold nights make rock surfaces crack and peel; (B) wind blows sand across the Thar desert and piles it into dunes. Which is weathering and which is erosion?
items.prompt_hi: Tulna karo: (A) Rajasthan mein garam din aur thandi raatein chattanon ki sataha mein daraar daal ke chhilka utaar deti hain; (B) hawa Thar registaan mein ret uda ke tibbe bana deti hai. Kaunsa weathering hai aur kaunsa erosion?
items.answer: A is weathering (rock breaking where it is); B is erosion, with the wind carrying sand and dropping it in dunes.
acceptable: a toot raha hai, b ud raha hai
hints: Ask in which case the rock pieces move
Point to 'break' versus 'move'
Prompt: A breaks the rock, so it is ___; B moves the sand, so it is ___
Assert: A is weathering, B is erosion

verified.solverAnswer: A is weathering (rock breaking in place); B is erosion (wind carrying and depositing sand).

items.prompt_en: A peepal tree is growing out of a crack in an old wall. What will happen to the wall over many years, and what is this an example of?
items.prompt_hi: Ek purani deewar ki daraar se peepal ka ped ug raha hai. Kai saalon mein deewar ka kya hoga, aur ye kiska example hai?
items.answer: The roots grow thicker and push the crack wider until the wall breaks apart; this is weathering by plants.
hints: Ask what roots do as they grow
Point to the crack getting wider
Prompt: growing roots ___ the crack, which is ___
Assert: roots widen cracks and break the wall; weathering by plants

verified.solverAnswer: Roots widen the crack and eventually break/damage the wall; weathering by plants (biological weathering).

items.prompt_en: After forests on a hill are cut down, villages below see muddier rivers and more landslides. Explain this using erosion.
items.prompt_hi: Pahadi ke jungle kaatne ke baad neeche ke gaon mein nadiyaan zyada matmaili ho jaati hain aur zyada landslide hote hain. Erosion se ise samjhao.
items.answer: Tree roots hold the soil together and leaves slow the rain; without trees, rain erodes the soil quickly, rivers carry the mud downhill, and loosened slopes slide.
hints: Ask what was holding the hill's soil before
Point to bare slopes in heavy rain
Prompt: without ___, rain erodes soil fast and slopes ___
Assert: cutting trees removes the roots that hold soil, so erosion and landslides increase

verified.solverAnswer: Without tree roots and leaf cover, rain erodes loose soil quickly into rivers (muddy) and slopes become unstable, causing landslides.

items.prompt_en: Tushar says, 'Soil is easy to replace; if rain washes it away, new soil will form by next year.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Tushar kehta hai, 'Mitti ko badalna aasaan hai; agar baarish use bahaa le jaaye, toh agle saal tak nayi mitti ban jaayegi.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: Soil forms very slowly from weathered rock and humus; a few centimetres can take hundreds of years, so lost soil cannot be replaced in a year.
hints: Ask how soil is made
Point to rock being weathered slowly
Prompt: a few centimetres of soil can take ___ of years
Assert: soil forms over hundreds of years, so it must be protected

verified.solverAnswer: Soil forms very slowly (centimetres take hundreds to thousands of years), so it can't be replaced in a year; protect it.

items.prompt_en: Draw a river's journey from the mountains to the sea in three parts. Label where you would find big sharp rocks, rounded pebbles, and fine sand and mud. Explain the pattern.
items.prompt_hi: Pahadon se samudra tak nadi ka safar teen hisson mein banao. Label karo ki bade nukile patthar, gol kankar, aur baarik ret aur keechad kahaan milenge. Pattern samjhao.
items.answer: Mountains: big sharp rocks, freshly broken. Middle: rounded pebbles, rubbed while being carried. Near the sea, on the plains and in the delta: fine sand and mud, dropped where the river slows (for example the Sundarbans delta).
hints: Invite them to draw the river first
Point to how pieces get smaller downstream
Prompt: sharp rocks up high, ___ pebbles in the middle, fine ___ near the sea
Assert: pieces get smaller and rounder downstream and are dropped where the river slows

verified.solverAnswer: Mountains: big sharp rocks; middle plains: rounded pebbles; near sea: fine sand and mud; pieces get smaller and rounder downstream as they are worn, and dropped where river slows.

items.prompt_en: Using the chalk-in-a-box experiment, explain to a friend how a mountain stream turns rocks into pebbles and sand.
items.prompt_hi: Chalk-in-a-box experiment ki madad se apne dost ko samjhao ki pahaadi nadi chattanon ko kankar aur ret mein kaise badal deti hai.
items.answer: Like the shaken chalk, rocks carried by a stream knock and rub against each other and the riverbed; over a long time their edges wear off, they get rounder and smaller, and finally break into sand.
hints: Invite them to start with what happened to the chalk
Point to the stream as a giant slow shaker
Prompt: knocking and rubbing make rocks ___ and ___
Assert: rubbing in moving water slowly turns rocks into pebbles and sand

verified.solverAnswer: Like chalk shaken in the box, rocks and pebbles knock and rub each other in fast water, wearing corners to round pebbles and finally sand.

items.prompt_en: From last time: name one thing that can break rocks without any people being involved.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: ek aisi cheez batao jo bina kisi insaan ke chattanon ko tod sakti hai.
items.answer: Any one of: water freezing in cracks, plant roots, heating and cooling, rainwater.
hints: Ask what happened to the frozen bottle
Point to the peepal in the wall
Prompt: ice in ___ or plant ___ can break rocks
Assert: freezing water, roots, heat and cold all weather rocks

verified.solverAnswer: Freezing water in cracks (ice), plant roots, wind, water, temperature changes.

workedExample.problem: Explain step by step how a sharp rock high in the Himalayas could end up as sand on a beach.
steps: Water seeps into a crack in the rock, freezes at night and expands, breaking off a sharp piece: weathering
The piece falls into a stream, and the water starts carrying it away: erosion
As it is carried, it knocks and rubs against other rocks and the riverbed, becoming rounder and smaller
Over a very long time and many kilometres, it breaks down into grains of sand
Where the river slows down near the sea, the sand is dropped on the shore or in the delta

The piece falls into a stream and is carried away: ___
It knocks and rubs against rocks, becoming ___ and smaller

skills.title: Describe adolescence (roughly 10 to 19 years) and puberty, and that the changes are brought about by hormones
List the physical changes of adolescence: growth spurt in height, voice change, new hair growth, more active sweat and oil glands, changes in body shape, and the start of periods in girls
Explain that the timing and speed of these changes differ from person to person, and that being early or late is normal

expectations: Adolescence is the stage of life between childhood and adulthood, roughly from 10 to 19 years of age.
The changes are brought about by chemical messengers called hormones; the part of adolescence in which the body matures so that it can later have children is called puberty.

Common physical changes: a sudden increase in height (growth spurt), a deeper voice (more noticeable in boys, whose voice box grows and may show as an Adam's apple), new hair growth such as in the underarms, more active sweat and oil glands (body odour, pimples), changes in body shape, and in girls the start of periods (menstruation).
These changes start at different ages and go at different speeds for different people; girls often start a little earlier than boys; being early or late is normal.
The changes are natural and healthy, and questions about them can be asked to parents, teachers, doctors or other trusted adults.

misconceptions.belief: Everyone goes through these changes at exactly the same age.
signs: Worries that something is wrong because a friend has grown and they have not
Says all 12-year-olds should look the same

diagnostic.prompt_en: Ravi is 13 and has grown a lot this year. His friend Sunil, also 13, has hardly grown. What is most likely true?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ravi 13 saal ka hai aur is saal bahut lamba ho gaya. Uska dost Sunil bhi 13 ka hai par zyada nahi badha. Sabse zyada kya sach hone ki sambhavna hai?

options.text: Something must be wrong with Sunil
Changes start at different ages; Sunil's growth spurt may simply come later
Sunil will never grow tall

remediation.representation: A multi-line height chart of five classmates whose steep 'jump' happens in different years
remediation.moveShape: Have the child find each person's jump year and notice that all of them end up growing

misconceptions.belief: Pimples come only from eating oily food or from being dirty.
signs: Blames samosas alone for pimples
Thinks a classmate with pimples does not wash

diagnostic.prompt_en: Why do many teenagers get pimples?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Bahut se teenagers ko pimples kyon hote hain?

options.text: Only because they eat oily food
Hormones make the skin's oil glands more active, and blocked pores can turn into pimples
Because they are dirty

remediation.representation: A simple skin diagram: an oil gland making more oil, a pore getting blocked, a pimple forming
remediation.moveShape: Ask what started the extra oil; connect it to hormones, and keep washing as care, not blame

misconceptions.belief: These changes happen only to one group: for example, only boys' voices change.
signs: Says girls' voices never change
Thinks only girls have growth spurts

diagnostic.prompt_en: During adolescence, whose voice changes?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Adolescence mein kiski aawaaz badalti hai?

options.text: Only boys'
Both boys' and girls' voices change, though it is usually more noticeable in boys
Nobody's voice really changes

remediation.representation: Two audio clips of a person speaking at 10 and at 16, for both a boy and a girl
remediation.moveShape: Let the child notice both changes, then say which is bigger and why the voice box matters

items.prompt_en: What is the stage of life between childhood and adulthood called, and roughly what ages does it cover?
items.prompt_hi: Bachpan aur badappan ke beech ke jeevan ke daur ko kya kehte hain, aur ye lagbhag kis umar tak hota hai?
items.answer: Adolescence; roughly from 10 to 19 years of age.
hints: Ask what we call the 'teen' years
Point to the ages between childhood and adulthood
Prompt: it is called ___ and lasts roughly from ___ to 19
Assert: adolescence, roughly ages 10 to 19

verified.solverAnswer: Adolescence; roughly 11 (or 10) to 19 years.

items.prompt_en: Name three physical changes that happen during adolescence.
items.prompt_hi: Adolescence ke dauraan hone wale teen shaaririk badlav batao.
items.answer: Any three of: a growth spurt in height, the voice getting deeper, new hair growth (for example in the underarms), more sweat and oil (body odour, pimples), changes in body shape, and periods starting in girls.
hints: Ask what the height chart on the wall shows over the years
Point to voice, skin and height
Prompt: height ___, voice gets ___, and new ___ grows
Assert: growth spurt, voice change and new hair are common changes

verified.solverAnswer: Growth spurt (height), voice change, new hair growth, pimples, more sweating, body shape changes.

items.prompt_en: On screen is a height chart of five friends from age 9 to 16, with the later years hidden. Before you see them, predict: will all five have their biggest growth jump in the same year?
items.prompt_hi: Screen pe paanch doston ka 9 se 16 saal tak ka height chart hai, aage ke saal chhupe hue hain. Dekhne se pehle guess karo: kya paanchon ki sabse badi lambai ki chhalaang ek hi saal mein hogi?
items.answer: No. Each friend has a growth spurt at a different age; girls often have it a little earlier than boys. Different timing is normal.
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason
Point to friends of the same age looking different heights
Prompt: growth spurts start at ___ ages
Assert: no; everyone's growth spurt comes at their own time

verified.solverAnswer: No; each person's growth spurt comes at different ages.

items.prompt_en: Your height mark on the wall was 135 cm at age 10 and 137 cm at 11. Predict: will you keep growing only 2 cm a year until you are 18?
items.prompt_hi: Deewar pe tumhari lambai ka nishaan 10 saal pe 135 cm aur 11 saal pe 137 cm tha. Guess karo: kya tum 18 saal tak har saal sirf 2 cm hi badhoge?
items.answer: Probably not. During the adolescent growth spurt many people grow much faster, sometimes several centimetres in a year; afterwards growth slows and usually stops by the late teens.
hints: Ask what 'growth spurt' means
Point to a steep part on a growth chart
Prompt: during the growth ___, people grow ___ for a while
Assert: growth speeds up in the spurt, then slows and stops

verified.solverAnswer: No; growth speeds up in the adolescent growth spurt (more than 2 cm/year) then slows and stops.

items.prompt_en: What causes the body to change during adolescence?
items.prompt_hi: Adolescence ke dauraan shareer mein badlav kis wajah se hote hain?
items.answer: Hormones: chemical messengers released into the blood that signal the body to grow and mature.
hints: Ask how one part of the body could send a message to the whole body
Point to messengers travelling in the blood
Prompt: chemical messengers called ___
Assert: hormones bring about the changes of adolescence

verified.solverAnswer: Hormones (released by glands) cause the changes.

items.prompt_en: Why do many adolescents notice more sweat and body odour, and what helps?
items.prompt_hi: Bahut se adolescents ko zyada paseena aur shareer ki gandh kyon mehsoos hoti hai, aur isme kya madad karta hai?
items.answer: Sweat glands become more active; bacteria on the skin act on sweat and cause the smell. A daily bath, washing the underarms, and clean clothes and socks help.
hints: Ask what changes about the sweat glands
Point to bacteria on the skin
Prompt: sweat glands get more ___; a daily ___ helps
Assert: more active sweat glands; bathing daily and clean clothes help

verified.solverAnswer: Sweat glands become more active and bacteria break down sweat; bathe daily, wear clean clothes, deodorant optional.

items.prompt_en: Compare how the voice changes in boys and in girls during adolescence.
items.prompt_hi: Adolescence mein ladkon aur ladkiyon ki aawaaz kaise badalti hai, tulna karo.
items.answer: Both voices get deeper. In boys the voice box grows more, so the voice becomes much deeper, may crack for a while, and an Adam's apple may show; in girls the change is smaller and less noticeable.
hints: Ask whether only one group's voice changes
Point to the voice box growing
Prompt: both voices get ___; it is more ___ in boys
Assert: both change; boys' voice deepens more because the voice box grows more

verified.solverAnswer: Both voices deepen; boys' more noticeable because the larynx/voice box grows more (Adam's apple); girls' change slightly.

items.prompt_en: Two cousins, Priya and Arjun, are both 12. At a family wedding, Priya is taller than Arjun this year, though last year Arjun was taller. Is this normal? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Do cousins, Priya aur Arjun, dono 12 saal ke hain. Ek shaadi mein Priya is saal Arjun se lambi hai, jabki pichhle saal Arjun lamba tha. Kya ye normal hai? Kyon?
items.answer: Yes. Girls often begin their growth spurt earlier than boys, so they can be taller for a while; boys often catch up and grow later.
hints: Ask who usually starts the growth spurt earlier
Point to boys catching up later
Prompt: girls often start the growth spurt ___
Assert: normal; girls often grow earlier and boys catch up later

verified.solverAnswer: Normal; girls often start growth spurt earlier than boys, boys catch up later.

items.prompt_en: A sports coach picks 12-year-olds for a team only by their height. Using what you know about adolescence, why might this be unfair?
items.prompt_hi: Ek sports coach 12 saal ke bachchon ko sirf unki lambai dekh ke team mein chunta hai. Adolescence ke baare mein jo jaante ho, uske hisaab se ye unfair kyon ho sakta hai?
items.answer: Children grow at different ages; a child who is short at 12 may grow a lot later. Height at 12 does not show final height or ability, so skill should be judged instead.
hints: Ask whether today's height is final
Point to late growth spurts
Prompt: a short child now may ___ later
Assert: growth timing varies, so height at 12 is an unfair test

verified.solverAnswer: Growth timing varies; a child who is short at 12 may grow later, so height at that age doesn't show potential.

items.prompt_en: Mohit says, 'Pimples come only from eating samosas, so if I stop eating them I'll never get pimples.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Mohit kehta hai, 'Pimples sirf samose khaane se hote hain, toh agar main samose band kar doon toh kabhi pimples nahi honge.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: Pimples in adolescence happen mainly because hormones make the skin's oil glands more active and pores get blocked. Gentle face washing and a balanced diet can help, but no single food is the only cause.
hints: Ask what changes in the skin during adolescence
Point to oil glands and blocked pores
Prompt: hormones make oil glands more ___
Assert: pimples come mainly from hormone-driven oil, not one food

verified.solverAnswer: Pimples are mainly due to hormones making oil glands more active and blocking pores; not just samosas; food may matter slightly but stopping won't prevent.

items.prompt_en: Draw a simple timeline from age 8 to 20. Mark roughly when the growth spurt often happens for many girls and for many boys, and when growth usually stops.
items.prompt_hi: 8 se 20 saal tak ki ek simple timeline banao. Lagbhag mark karo ki kai ladkiyon aur kai ladkon ki growth spurt aksar kab hoti hai, aur lambai badhna aam taur pe kab rukta hai.
items.answer: Many girls: roughly 10 to 13; many boys: roughly 12 to 15; growth usually stops in the late teens. These are rough ranges, and each person is different.
hints: Invite them to draw the line with ages marked
Point to girls' range starting a little earlier
Prompt: girls often around ___, boys often around ___, stopping in the late ___
Assert: girls often earlier, boys a bit later, growth ends in the late teens; everyone differs

verified.solverAnswer: Timeline 8-20: girls' spurt often about 10-13; boys' about 12-15; growth usually stops late teens (about 18-19); everyone differs.

items.prompt_en: Your younger cousin is worried because her friends have started growing faster than her. Explain to her why this is normal.
items.prompt_hi: Tumhari chhoti cousin pareshaan hai kyonki uske dost usse jaldi lambe hone lage hain. Use samjhao ki ye normal kyon hai.
items.answer: Everyone's body changes when its own hormones start the changes, which can be at different ages over several years; starting later is normal, and her growth spurt will come. She can ask a parent or doctor anything she wants to know.
hints: Invite them to begin with what starts the changes
Point to the height chart with different jump years
Prompt: changes start at ___ ages, and later is ___
Assert: different timing is normal; her turn will come

verified.solverAnswer: Everyone starts growing at different ages; later start is normal and she'll catch up.

items.prompt_en: From last time: what are the chemical messengers that bring about the changes of adolescence called?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: adolescence ke badlav laane wale chemical messengers ko kya kehte hain?
items.answer: Hormones.
hints: Ask what travels in the blood to carry the message
Point to the word starting with 'h'
Prompt: they are called ___
Assert: hormones

verified.solverAnswer: Hormones.

skills.title: Identify emotional and social changes in adolescence: mood changes, wanting independence, caring more about looks and friends' opinions
Name trusted people and safe places to talk to (parents, teachers, school counsellors, doctors, elder siblings, helplines 1098 and 14416)
Choose healthy ways to handle stress and peer pressure: talking, sleep, activity, hobbies, saying no and walking away

expectations: In adolescence, feelings can change quickly (mood swings), and many young people want more independence and care more about how they look and what friends think.
These feelings are a normal part of growing up, linked to hormones and to the many changes happening in life.

It is healthy and not shameful to talk about worries and body changes with trusted adults: parents, teachers, school counsellors, doctors or elder siblings; information should come from them or a good textbook, not just rumours.
Anyone who feels very sad for a long time, or is hurt or unsafe, should tell a trusted adult straight away; in India, Childline (1098) and Tele-MANAS (14416) are free helplines.
Peer pressure can push people towards harmful things like tobacco; it is okay to say no and walk away, and real friends respect that.
Enough sleep, physical activity, hobbies and talking things over help manage stress and moods.

misconceptions.belief: It is wrong or shameful to talk about these changes.

Laughs at or teases classmates who ask

Check it with a trusted adult, a doctor, or your science teacher or textbook
