verified.solverAnswer: They also have a multi-chambered stomach (a rumen-like chamber) for storing and digesting grass, unlike our single-chambered stomach (camels have three chambers).
verified.note: ACCURACY (minor): key says camels have a stomach 'with a rumen'; camels are pseudo-ruminants (3 compartments, no true rumen). Goat part is correct. Fine at class-7 level but should say 'a rumen-like chamber'.

items.prompt_en: Draw arrows (or describe) the path of grass in a cow: mouth, rumen, back to mouth as cud, then onward. Where are microbes most important?
items.prompt_hi: Gaay mein ghaas ka raasta teer se dikhaao (ya batao): munh, rumen, phir cud banke wapas munh, phir aage. Microbes sabse zyada kahaan kaam aate hain?
items.answer: Mouth to rumen (stored, microbes partly digest cellulose) to mouth again (cud chewed) to the other stomach chambers to intestines. Microbes matter most in the rumen.
acceptable: mouth, rumen, mouth, rest of stomach; microbes in rumen
hints: Ask where the grass goes first
Point to the arrow that loops back
Prompt: microbes work mainly in the ___
Assert: mouth, rumen, mouth (cud), onward; microbes in the rumen

verified.solverAnswer: Mouth (quick chewing) to rumen (stored, microbes begin digesting) back to mouth as cud (rechewed) then swallowed to other stomach chambers and intestines; microbes matter most in the rumen.

items.prompt_en: A hummingbird's beak is long and thin, a parrot's is short and strongly hooked. Without being told, guess what each mainly eats and explain your reasoning.
items.prompt_hi: Hummingbird ki chonch lambi aur patli hoti hai, tote ki chhoti aur mudi hui, mazboot. Bina bataye guess karo har ek mainly kya khaata hai aur kyun.
items.answer: Hummingbird: nectar from deep flowers, as the long thin beak reaches inside. Parrot: hard seeds, nuts and fruits, which the strong hooked beak can crack.
acceptable: hummingbird nectar, parrot nuts and seeds
hints: Ask what a long thin tool is good for
Point to the parrot cracking a hard shell
Prompt: the beak shape matches the ___
Assert: long thin for nectar; strong hooked for cracking seeds

verified.solverAnswer: Hummingbird eats nectar (long thin beak reaches into flowers); parrot eats seeds, nuts, fruits (strong hooked beak cracks/shells them); beak shape fits food.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend from the city who has never seen a cow up close why cows keep chewing even after they stop grazing.
items.prompt_hi: Shahar ke dost ko, jisne kabhi gaay paas se nahi dekhi, samjhao ki gaay charna band karne ke baad bhi kyun chabaati rehti hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: the cow swallows grass quickly into the rumen; microbes there partly digest it; it brings back the cud to chew again; this helps digest tough cellulose that humans cannot digest.
hints: Ask where the grass first goes
What makes grass hard to digest?
Prompt: it brings back the ___ to chew
Assert: rumen storage, microbes, re-chewing cud to digest cellulose

verified.solverAnswer: Cow swallows grass quickly into rumen; later brings back cud to chew again to break tough cellulose and help microbes digest; this is rumination.

items.prompt_en: From memory: what is the bag inside an amoeba where food is digested called?
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: amoeba ke andar woh thaili jismein khaana pachta hai, kya kehlaati hai?
items.answer: The food vacuole.
hints: It forms when food is engulfed
It is a small 'bag' or space
Prompt: food ___
Assert: food vacuole

verified.solverAnswer: Food vacuole.

workedExample.problem: How does a cow get food from grass?
steps: Graze: the cow swallows grass quickly with little chewing
Store: the grass goes to the rumen, the first chamber of its stomach
Partly digest: microbes in the rumen begin breaking down cellulose
Re-chew: lumps of cud come back to the mouth and are chewed thoroughly
Finish: the chewed food moves through the other stomach chambers and intestines, where digestion and absorption are completed
fadedVersion: Graze: the cow ___ grass quickly
Store: the grass goes to the ___
Partly digest: ___ break down cellulose
Re-chew: lumps of ___ come back to the mouth
Finish: digestion and ___ are completed in the intestines

skills.title: Distinguish breathing (taking air in and out) from respiration (using oxygen to release energy from food in cells)
Describe the breathing process and compare inhaled and exhaled air
Explain how breathing rate changes with activity and how other animals breathe (gills, skin, spiracles)

expectations: Breathing is the movement of air into and out of the lungs; respiration is the process in every cell in which food (glucose) is broken down, usually using oxygen, to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water.
When we breathe in, the chest expands and the diaphragm moves down, and air enters the lungs; when we breathe out, the chest returns and air is pushed out.
Inhaled air and exhaled air both are mostly nitrogen; exhaled air has less oxygen (about 16% instead of about 21%) and more carbon dioxide (about 4% instead of a tiny amount) and more water vapour.
During exercise the muscles need more energy, so they respire faster; we breathe faster and deeper to supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide.

Different animals breathe in different ways: fish use gills to take oxygen dissolved in water, earthworms breathe through their moist skin, insects through tiny holes called spiracles and air tubes, and frogs through lungs and skin.

misconceptions.belief: Breathing and respiration are the same thing.
signs: Uses the words interchangeably
Says respiration happens only in the lungs
Cannot say what respiration releases

diagnostic.prompt_en: Where does respiration (using oxygen to release energy from food) actually take place?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Respiration (oxygen se khaane mein se energy nikaalna) asal mein kahaan hota hai?

options.text: Only in the lungs
In every cell of the body
Only in the nose

remediation.representation: Two-level picture: lungs (breathing, air exchange) and a single cell (respiration, glucose + oxygen to energy)
remediation.moveShape: Ask what the leg muscle cell needs oxygen for; trace oxygen from lungs to blood to cell

misconceptions.belief: We breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.
signs: Says 'we inhale oxygen and exhale carbon dioxide' as pure gases
Surprised that exhaled air still has oxygen (used in mouth-to-mouth rescue breathing)

diagnostic.prompt_en: What is the main gas in the air you breathe out?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Jo hawa tum saans chhodte waqt bahar nikaalte ho, usmein sabse zyada kaunsi gas hoti hai?

options.text: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen, with still quite a lot of oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air
Only oxygen

remediation.representation: Two bar charts side by side: inhaled vs exhaled air (nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapour)
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to predict each bar before revealing; focus on how little the nitrogen bar changes

misconceptions.belief: Fish and other water animals do not need oxygen, or they breathe in water as their 'air' without using oxygen.
signs: Says fish don't breathe
Thinks gills take in water itself as the needed gas

diagnostic.prompt_en: Why do fish in a small, crowded, unaerated tank come to the surface and gulp?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Chhote, bheed wale, bina air pump ke tank mein machhliyan upar aakar munh kyun maarti hain?

options.text: They are hungry
The water has too little dissolved oxygen, and fish need oxygen taken in through gills
Fish do not need oxygen, they are just playing

remediation.representation: A fish gill picture with dissolved oxygen bubbles moving from water into blood
remediation.moveShape: Contrast the fish's gills with our lungs: same job, different medium

items.prompt_en: Count your breaths for one minute while sitting quietly. Then predict: after running on the spot for one minute, will your breaths per minute go up, go down or stay the same? Then try it and count.
items.prompt_hi: Shaant baith ke ek minute tak apni saansein gino. Phir guess karo: ek minute ek jagah daudne ke baad saansein per minute badhengi, ghatengi ya utni hi rahengi? Phir karke gino.
items.answer: They go up (for example from about 15-20 to 30 or more per minute), because the muscles are respiring faster and need more oxygen and must remove more carbon dioxide.
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason before running
Point to the muscles working harder
Prompt: working muscles need more ___
Assert: breathing rate rises to supply more oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Breathing rate goes up because working muscles need more oxygen and release more carbon dioxide.

items.prompt_en: Breathe out onto a cold steel plate or a mirror. Before you do, predict what you will see, and what it tells you about exhaled air.
items.prompt_hi: Thandi steel ki plate ya sheeshe pe saans chhodo. Karne se pehle guess karo kya dikhega, aur usse bahar ki saans ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai.
items.answer: A misty layer of tiny water droplets forms, showing that exhaled air contains water vapour.
hints: Ask for a guess first
Point to what happens to a cold glass of water on a humid day
Prompt: exhaled air contains water ___
Assert: mist forms because exhaled air has water vapour

verified.solverAnswer: Mist/tiny water droplets form on the cold surface; exhaled air contains water vapour that condenses.

items.prompt_en: Say whether each is breathing or respiration: (a) your chest rises and falls (b) a muscle cell breaks down glucose to get energy (c) air goes in through your nose.
items.prompt_hi: Batao har ek breathing hai ya respiration: (a) chhaati upar-neeche hoti hai (b) muscle cell glucose todke energy leta hai (c) hawa naak se andar jaati hai.
items.answer: (a) breathing (b) respiration (c) breathing.
acceptable: a breathing, b respiration, c breathing
hints: Ask which one happens inside a cell
Point to (a) and (c) being about air moving
Prompt: energy from food in a cell is ___
Assert: a and c breathing; b respiration

verified.solverAnswer: (a) breathing; (b) respiration; (c) breathing.

items.prompt_en: Why do we need oxygen at all? What would stop if oxygen did not reach our cells?
items.prompt_hi: Humein oxygen ki zaroorat hi kyun hai? Agar oxygen cells tak na pahunche toh kya ruk jaayega?
items.answer: Cells use oxygen to break down food (glucose) and release the energy needed for every activity; without it, cells cannot release enough energy and stop working.
acceptable: to release energy from food in cells
hints: Ask what every activity needs
Point to food being the fuel and oxygen helping burn it slowly
Prompt: oxygen helps cells release ___ from food
Assert: respiration in cells uses oxygen to release energy

verified.solverAnswer: Cells use oxygen to release energy from food (respiration); without oxygen, cells could not release energy, so body activities and life stop.

items.prompt_en: Compare inhaled and exhaled air for oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
items.prompt_hi: Andar li gayi aur bahar chhodi gayi hawa ki oxygen, carbon dioxide aur paani ki bhaap ke liye tulna karo.
items.answer: Exhaled air has less oxygen (about 16% vs 21%), much more carbon dioxide (about 4% vs about 0.04%) and more water vapour; nitrogen stays about the same.
acceptable: less oxygen, more carbon dioxide, more water vapour
hints: Ask which gas the cells use up
Which gas do cells make?
Prompt: exhaled air has ___ oxygen and ___ carbon dioxide
Assert: less oxygen, more carbon dioxide and water vapour

verified.solverAnswer: Inhaled air: more oxygen (about 21%), less CO2 (0.04%), little water vapour. Exhaled air: less oxygen (about 16%), more CO2 (about 4%), more water vapour.

items.prompt_en: A poster says: 'We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide.' What is incomplete or misleading about this?
items.prompt_hi: Ek poster kehta hai: 'Hum oxygen andar lete hain aur carbon dioxide bahar chhodte hain.' Ismein kya adhoora ya galat-fehmi wala hai?
items.answer: We breathe in air (mostly nitrogen, about 21% oxygen) and breathe out air that is still mostly nitrogen with about 16% oxygen; the change is less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, not pure gases.
acceptable: we breathe air, not pure gases
hints: Ask what most of the air is made of
Point to rescue breathing working because exhaled air still has oxygen
Prompt: both are mostly ___
Assert: we breathe air; exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide

verified.solverAnswer: We breathe in air (mostly nitrogen); not all oxygen is used; exhaled air has less oxygen and more CO2 and water vapour; also respiration happens in cells.

items.prompt_en: Place your hands on your ribs and breathe deeply. Describe what your ribs and chest do when you breathe in and out, and link it to a balloon diagram of the lungs.
items.prompt_hi: Apne haath pasliyon pe rakho aur gehri saans lo. Batao saans lete aur chhodte waqt pasliyaan aur chhaati kya karti hain, aur ise phephdon ke balloon wale chitra se jodo.
items.answer: Breathing in: ribs move up and out, the diaphragm moves down, the chest space gets bigger and air rushes in, like balloons filling. Breathing out: ribs move down and in, the diaphragm moves up, space gets smaller and air is pushed out.
acceptable: in: chest expands, air enters; out: chest shrinks, air leaves
hints: Ask what your hands feel when you breathe in
Point to the chest getting bigger
Prompt: bigger chest space means air rushes ___
Assert: chest expands to breathe in, contracts to breathe out

verified.solverAnswer: Breathing in: ribs move up and out, diaphragm flattens/moves down, chest cavity enlarges and air rushes into lungs (balloons inflate); breathing out: ribs down, diaphragm up, chest shrinks, air pushed out.

items.prompt_en: After heavy rain, earthworms come up onto the surface of the soil. Using how earthworms breathe, suggest a reason.
items.prompt_hi: Tez baarish ke baad kenchue mitti ki sateh pe aa jaate hain. Kenchue kaise saans lete hain, isse ek kaaran socho.
items.answer: Earthworms breathe through their moist skin, taking oxygen from air in the soil; when soil fills with water there is less air, so they come up to get oxygen.
acceptable: breathe through skin; waterlogged soil has little air
hints: Ask how an earthworm breathes
Point to air spaces in the soil filling with water
Prompt: soaked soil has less ___
Assert: they surface to get oxygen because waterlogged soil has little air

verified.solverAnswer: Water fills air spaces in soil, so little oxygen for breathing through skin; worms come up to get oxygen.

items.prompt_en: Mountaineers climbing very high in the Himalaya often breathe faster even when walking slowly, and some carry oxygen cylinders. Explain.
items.prompt_hi: Himalaya mein bahut oonchaai pe chadhne wale log dheere chalte hue bhi tez saans lete hain, aur kuch oxygen cylinder le jaate hain. Samjhao.
items.answer: At high altitude the air is thinner, so each breath brings in less oxygen; the body breathes faster to get enough oxygen for respiration in cells, and cylinders supply extra oxygen.
acceptable: thin air has less oxygen per breath
hints: Ask what changes in the air high up
Point to cells still needing the same oxygen
Prompt: each breath gives ___ oxygen
Assert: less oxygen per breath, so faster breathing or extra oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Air high up has less oxygen per breath (low pressure), so breathe faster and deeper, cylinders supply extra oxygen.

items.prompt_en: Compare how a fish, a cockroach and a frog take in oxygen.
items.prompt_hi: Machhli, cockroach aur medhak oxygen kaise lete hain, compare karo.
items.answer: Fish: gills take oxygen dissolved in water. Cockroach: air enters through spiracles (small holes) into air tubes. Frog: lungs, and also through its moist skin.
acceptable: fish gills, cockroach spiracles, frog lungs and skin
hints: Ask where a fish gets oxygen from
Point to tiny holes along an insect's body
Prompt: fish ___, cockroach ___, frog ___ and skin
Assert: gills, spiracles and air tubes, lungs and skin

verified.solverAnswer: Fish: gills take dissolved oxygen from water; cockroach: spiracles and air tubes (tracheae); frog: lungs and moist skin.

items.prompt_en: Your younger sister says 'breathing and respiration are the same'. Explain the difference to her with an example.
items.prompt_hi: Chhoti behen kehti hai 'breathing aur respiration ek hi hai'. Use ek example se farak samjhao.
items.answer: Key ideas: breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration happens in every cell, using oxygen to break down food and release energy, giving carbon dioxide; example: running makes muscle cells respire faster, so we breathe faster.
acceptable: breathing is air movement; respiration is energy release in cells
hints: Ask where breathing happens
Ask where respiration happens
Prompt: give an example like ___
Assert: breathing in lungs; respiration in cells releases energy

verified.solverAnswer: Breathing is taking air in and out of lungs; respiration happens in cells, using oxygen to release energy from glucose; e.g. breathing is the bellows, respiration is the fire.

items.prompt_en: From memory: name the tiny holes on the body of an insect through which air enters.
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: keede ke shareer pe woh chhote chhed jinse hawa andar jaati hai, kya kehlaate hain?
items.answer: Spiracles.
hints: They are along the sides of the body
The word starts with 'sp'
Prompt: ___
Assert: spiracles

verified.solverAnswer: Spiracles.

workedExample.problem: Why do you breathe faster after climbing stairs quickly?
steps: Activity: leg muscles work hard and need more energy
Respiration: muscle cells break down more glucose with oxygen to release that energy
Demand: the cells need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide
Response: breathing becomes faster and deeper to take in more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide
Recovery: after rest, energy demand falls and breathing slows back down
fadedVersion: Activity: leg muscles need more ___
Respiration: cells break down glucose using ___
Demand: cells need more oxygen and make more ___
Response: breathing becomes ___ and deeper
Recovery: after rest, breathing ___ down

skills.title: State that green plants make their own food (glucose, stored as starch) by photosynthesis in leaves
Name the raw materials and conditions (carbon dioxide, water, sunlight, chlorophyll) and the products (glucose/starch and oxygen)
Interpret the starch test on a partly covered leaf as evidence for the need for sunlight and chlorophyll
Explain that plants respire all the time, day and night, while photosynthesis happens only in light

expectations: Green plants make their own food; this process is photosynthesis and it happens mainly in the leaves.
In photosynthesis, the green pigment chlorophyll uses the energy of sunlight to combine carbon dioxide (from the air) and water (from the soil) into glucose; oxygen is released.
Glucose is turned into starch and stored; a leaf that has made food turns blue-black when tested with iodine.
Soil gives plants water and minerals, not their food; most of a plant's mass comes from carbon dioxide from the air and water.
Like all living things, plants respire all the time, day and night, using oxygen to release energy from food; in sunlight photosynthesis is faster, so a leaf gives out more oxygen than it uses.

misconceptions.belief: Plants get their food from the soil, through their roots.
signs: Says 'roots eat food from the soil'
Calls fertiliser 'plant food' and thinks that is the whole story
Expects the soil in a pot to get used up as the plant grows

diagnostic.prompt_en: A small plant is grown in a pot of soil for five years and becomes a large plant. The soil is weighed before and after. What would you expect?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek chhota paudha gamle ki mitti mein paanch saal ugaaya gaya aur bada ho gaya. Mitti ko pehle aur baad mein taula gaya. Kya ummeed karoge?

options.text: The soil lost about as much mass as the plant gained, because the plant ate the soil
The soil lost only a very little mass; the plant's mass came mainly from air (carbon dioxide) and water
The soil got heavier

remediation.representation: Before-after balance picture: tiny loss in soil mass beside a huge gain in plant mass, with arrows from air (CO2) and water
remediation.moveShape: Ask where the extra mass could have come from if not the soil; list the inputs one by one

misconceptions.belief: Plants do not respire, or they respire only at night.
signs: Says 'plants breathe in carbon dioxide and we breathe in oxygen'
Thinks plants switch from photosynthesis to respiration at sunset

diagnostic.prompt_en: When does a mango tree respire?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Aam ka ped respiration kab karta hai?

options.text: Only at night
All the time, day and night
Never; only animals respire

remediation.representation: A 24-hour timeline with two bars: respiration running all day and night, photosynthesis only in daylight and taller than respiration
remediation.moveShape: Ask what every living cell needs energy for, including root cells deep in dark soil

misconceptions.belief: Sunlight is itself the plant's food, or plants only need light, not carbon dioxide.
signs: Says 'plants eat sunlight'
Leaves out carbon dioxide when listing what plants need

diagnostic.prompt_en: What does a green leaf use to make glucose?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hara patta glucose banaane ke liye kya use karta hai?

options.text: Only sunlight
Carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of sunlight captured by chlorophyll
Soil and minerals

remediation.representation: A 'recipe card': ingredients (carbon dioxide, water), energy source (sunlight), kitchen (leaf with chlorophyll), dish (glucose) and by-product (oxygen)
remediation.moveShape: Have the child sort cards into ingredients vs energy vs products

items.prompt_en: A potted plant is kept in sunlight. A strip of black paper is clipped over part of one leaf, on both sides, for two days. Then the teacher tests the leaf for starch with iodine. Predict which part turns blue-black and which does not.
items.prompt_hi: Ek gamle ka paudha dhoop mein rakha hai. Ek patte ke kuch hisse pe dono taraf kaala kaagaz do din ke liye clip kar diya. Phir teacher iodine se patte mein starch test karti hain. Guess karo kaunsa hissa neela-kaala hoga aur kaunsa nahi.
items.answer: The uncovered part turns blue-black (starch present); the covered part does not, because without sunlight it could not make food.
acceptable: uncovered part blue-black, covered part not
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason first
Point to which part could get sunlight
Prompt: no sunlight means no ___
Assert: uncovered part shows starch; covered part does not

verified.solverAnswer: Uncovered part turns blue-black (starch present); covered part doesn't (no photosynthesis without light).

items.prompt_en: A famous experiment: a 2.5 kg willow sapling was grown in a tub of soil for five years, given only water. It grew to about 75 kg. Predict how much soil was lost: about 72 kg, about 7 kg, or only about 60 grams?
items.prompt_hi: Ek mashhoor experiment: 2.5 kg ka willow ka paudha mitti ke tub mein paanch saal tak ugaaya gaya, sirf paani diya gaya. Woh lagbhag 75 kg ka ho gaya. Guess karo kitni mitti kam hui: lagbhag 72 kg, 7 kg, ya sirf 60 gram?
items.answer: Only about 60 grams; almost none of the tree's mass came from the soil. It came from carbon dioxide in the air and water, through photosynthesis.
hints: Ask for a guess before the reveal
Point to how little the soil changed
Prompt: the mass came from ___ and ___
Assert: soil lost only about 60 g; mass came from air and water

verified.solverAnswer: Only about 60 g of soil lost; the plant's mass came mainly from water and carbon dioxide (air).
verified.note: ACCURACY (minor): figures rounded away from the real van Helmont data (about 2.3 kg to 76.7 kg, soil lost about 57 g); conclusion unaffected.

items.prompt_en: Name the four things a green leaf needs for photosynthesis.
items.prompt_hi: Photosynthesis ke liye hare patte ko kaunsi chaar cheezein chahiye?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll.
hints: Ask what comes from the air
And what comes from the roots?
Prompt: CO2, ___, sunlight and the green ___
Assert: carbon dioxide, water, sunlight, chlorophyll

verified.solverAnswer: Carbon dioxide, water, sunlight, chlorophyll.

items.prompt_en: Complete in words: carbon dioxide + water, in sunlight with chlorophyll, gives ___ + ___.
items.prompt_hi: Words mein poora karo: carbon dioxide + paani, dhoop aur chlorophyll ke saath, se ___ + ___ banta hai.
items.answer: Glucose (food, stored as starch) + oxygen.
hints: One product is food
The other is a gas we breathe
Prompt: ___ and oxygen
Assert: glucose and oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Glucose (food) + oxygen.

items.prompt_en: If soil does not give plants food, why do farmers add manure and fertilisers?
items.prompt_hi: Agar mitti paudhon ko khaana nahi deti, toh kisaan khaad aur fertiliser kyun daalte hain?
items.answer: They supply minerals such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium that plants need in small amounts to grow healthily and make proteins and chlorophyll; the food itself is made by photosynthesis.
hints: Ask what else roots take up besides water
Point to minerals like nitrogen
Prompt: fertilisers give ___, not food
Assert: manure and fertilisers supply minerals; food comes from photosynthesis

verified.solverAnswer: Fertilisers and manure add minerals (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) the plant needs, not food itself; plants make food by photosynthesis.

items.prompt_en: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in a plant: when each happens, what goes in and what comes out.
items.prompt_hi: Paudhe mein photosynthesis aur respiration ki tulna karo: kab hota hai, kya andar jaata hai, kya bahar aata hai.
items.answer: Photosynthesis: only in light; carbon dioxide and water in, glucose and oxygen out. Respiration: all the time; glucose and oxygen used, carbon dioxide, water and energy released.
acceptable: photosynthesis in light makes food and oxygen; respiration always uses food and oxygen
hints: Ask which one needs sunlight
Ask which one happens in every cell all the time
Prompt: they are almost ___ of each other
Assert: photosynthesis in light only; respiration always

verified.solverAnswer: Photosynthesis: in light, in green parts; takes in CO2 and water, gives glucose and oxygen, stores energy. Respiration: day and night in all cells; takes in oxygen and glucose, gives CO2, water and energy.

items.prompt_en: Rohan says: 'Plants are so useful because they only take in carbon dioxide and only give out oxygen.' What is wrong with this?
items.prompt_hi: Rohan kehta hai: 'Paudhe isliye useful hain kyunki woh sirf carbon dioxide lete hain aur sirf oxygen dete hain.' Ismein kya galat hai?
items.answer: Plants also respire all the time, taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide; in daylight photosynthesis is faster, so overall they give out more oxygen, but not 'only' oxygen.
hints: Ask whether plant cells need energy
Point to respiration happening at night too
Prompt: plants also ___ day and night
Assert: plants respire too; overall in daylight they release more oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Plants also respire all the time, using oxygen and giving CO2; in daylight photosynthesis exceeds respiration so net oxygen release.

items.prompt_en: Why are most leaves broad and flat, and why are they green?
items.prompt_hi: Zyada-tar patte chaude aur chapte kyun hote hain, aur hare kyun?
items.answer: Broad, flat leaves capture more sunlight and have more surface for gas exchange; they are green because they contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the light energy needed for photosynthesis.
hints: Ask what a solar panel shape tells you
Point to the green pigment
Prompt: flat to catch ___; green because of ___
Assert: more light captured; chlorophyll makes them green

verified.solverAnswer: Broad flat leaves catch more sunlight and CO2; green due to chlorophyll that absorbs light for photosynthesis.

items.prompt_en: The leaves of a croton plant are red and yellow with little green. Can they still make food? What is your evidence-based guess?
items.prompt_hi: Croton ke patte laal aur peele hote hain, hara kam. Kya woh bhi khaana bana sakte hain? Saboot ke saath guess karo.
items.answer: Yes, they still contain chlorophyll, but its green colour is masked by other red and yellow pigments; they make food, though the parts truly lacking chlorophyll (pure white patches) would not.
acceptable: yes, chlorophyll is hidden by other colours
hints: Ask whether a different colour means no chlorophyll at all
Point to other pigments covering the green
Prompt: chlorophyll is present but ___
Assert: yes; chlorophyll is masked by other pigments

verified.solverAnswer: Yes; chlorophyll is still present, masked by red/yellow pigments; they photosynthesise.

items.prompt_en: Astronauts want to grow lettuce on a space station. List what the plants must be given, and explain why soil itself is not essential.
items.prompt_hi: Astronauts space station pe salad ke patte ugaana chahte hain. Batao paudhon ko kya-kya dena padega, aur mitti khud kyun zaroori nahi.
items.answer: Light (lamps), carbon dioxide, water, and minerals dissolved in water; soil is not essential because it only provides support, water and minerals, which can be supplied another way, as in hydroponics.
acceptable: light, carbon dioxide, water, minerals; soil not needed
hints: Ask what photosynthesis needs
What does soil normally supply?
Prompt: give light, CO2, water and ___
Assert: light, carbon dioxide, water, minerals; soil can be replaced

verified.solverAnswer: Light, carbon dioxide, water and minerals (nutrients); soil just supports roots and supplies water and minerals, which can be given in water (hydroponics).

items.prompt_en: Draw a leaf with arrows (or describe it): what enters the leaf, from where, and what leaves it, during photosynthesis on a sunny day.
items.prompt_hi: Ek patta banao teer ke saath (ya batao): dhoop wale din photosynthesis mein kya patte mein aata hai, kahaan se, aur kya bahar jaata hai.
items.answer: Sunlight falls on the leaf; carbon dioxide enters from the air through stomata; water comes from the roots through the stem; oxygen leaves through stomata; glucose is made and sent to other parts or stored as starch.
acceptable: CO2 and water in, oxygen out, glucose made
hints: Ask where carbon dioxide comes from
And water?
Prompt: oxygen goes out through the ___
Assert: CO2 and water in, oxygen out, glucose made

verified.solverAnswer: CO2 enters through stomata from air; water comes up from roots via veins; sunlight absorbed by chlorophyll; oxygen exits through stomata and glucose made.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend how a mango tree makes the food that ends up as sweet mangoes.
items.prompt_hi: Ek dost ko samjhao ki aam ka ped woh khaana kaise banaata hai jo aakhir meethe aam ban jaata hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: leaves with chlorophyll capture sunlight; they combine carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots into glucose; oxygen is released; the sugar is carried to the fruit and stored; soil gives water and minerals, not food.
acceptable: leaves, sunlight, CO2, water, glucose, oxygen, carried to fruit
hints: Ask where the food is made
What are the raw materials?
Prompt: the sugar is carried from the leaves to the ___
Assert: photosynthesis in leaves makes sugar that reaches the fruit

verified.solverAnswer: Leaves make sugar by photosynthesis from CO2, water and sunlight; sugar travels to fruit and is stored making sweet mango.

items.prompt_en: From memory: what colour does iodine turn when starch is present?
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: starch hone pe iodine kis rang ka ho jaata hai?
items.answer: Blue-black.
hints: Think of the leaf starch test
It is a very dark colour
Prompt: blue-___
Assert: blue-black

verified.solverAnswer: Blue-black.

workedExample.problem: Show that a leaf needs sunlight to make starch.
steps: Keep a potted plant in the dark for two days so its leaves use up their stored starch
Cover part of one leaf on both sides with black paper; keep the plant in sunlight for a few hours
The teacher removes the leaf, takes out its green colour, and adds iodine solution
Observe: the uncovered part turns blue-black; the covered part does not
Conclude: starch was made only where light reached, so sunlight is needed for photosynthesis
fadedVersion: Keep the plant in the ___ first so stored starch is used up
Cover part of a leaf with ___ paper; keep in sunlight
The teacher removes the green colour and adds ___
Observe: the uncovered part turns ___
Conclude: ___ is needed for photosynthesis

skills.title: Describe stomata as tiny pores on leaves, each opened and closed by two guard cells
Explain which gases pass through stomata in light and in darkness
Explain transpiration as loss of water vapour through stomata and why it matters

expectations: Stomata are tiny pores, mostly on the lower surface of leaves; each is surrounded by two guard cells that open and close it.
Gases enter and leave the leaf through stomata: carbon dioxide in and oxygen out during photosynthesis; oxygen in and carbon dioxide out for respiration.
In sunlight a leaf takes in more carbon dioxide than it gives out and releases more oxygen than it uses; in darkness only respiration happens, so it takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide.
Water vapour also escapes through stomata; this is transpiration, which cools the plant and helps pull water up from the roots.
Stomata often close in very hot, dry conditions to save water.

misconceptions.belief: Plants take in only carbon dioxide and never oxygen.
signs: Says leaves 'breathe in carbon dioxide' as their only gas
Is surprised that a plant in darkness takes in oxygen

diagnostic.prompt_en: A leaf is kept in complete darkness overnight. Which gas will it take in through its stomata?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek patta poori raat andhere mein rakha hai. Woh stomata se kaunsi gas andar lega?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, because plants only take in carbon dioxide
Oxygen, for respiration
No gas at all at night

remediation.representation: Day/night split leaf: in daylight big CO2-in and O2-out arrows plus small respiration arrows; at night only O2-in, CO2-out
remediation.moveShape: Ask what the leaf cells need all night long

misconceptions.belief: Stomata are always open holes, or there is no exchange of gases at night.
signs: Draws stomata as fixed holes
Says 'at night the leaf stops completely'

diagnostic.prompt_en: On a very hot dry afternoon, what may stomata do, and why?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Bahut garam sookhi dopahar mein stomata kya kar sakte hain, aur kyun?

options.text: Nothing; stomata are fixed holes
Close partly, so the plant loses less water
Open wider to drink water from the air

remediation.representation: Guard-cell animation: two bean-shaped cells swelling (open) and going limp (closed)
remediation.moveShape: Link to the child's own sweating: the plant controls water loss by closing pores

misconceptions.belief: Water only leaves a plant if it is spilled or the plant is cut; leaves do not lose water.
signs: Does not believe plants 'sweat'
Cannot explain the droplets inside a bag over a plant

diagnostic.prompt_en: A clear plastic bag is tied over a leafy branch in the sun for a few hours. Droplets appear inside the bag. Where did the water come from?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Dhoop mein ek patteedaar daali pe saaf plastic ki thaili baandhi gayi. Kuch ghanton mein thaili ke andar boondein aa gayi. Paani kahaan se aaya?

options.text: From the leaves, as water vapour through stomata (transpiration)
From the plastic bag itself
It rained inside the bag

remediation.representation: Bag-over-branch picture with a dry bag over a twig without leaves as a comparison
remediation.moveShape: Contrast the leafy and leafless bags; ask what made the difference

items.prompt_en: Tie a clean, dry, clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a potted plant and leave it in sunlight for 2-3 hours. Before you check, predict what you will see inside the bag.
items.prompt_hi: Gamle ke paudhe ki ek patteedaar daali pe saaf, sookhi, transparent plastic ki thaili baandho aur 2-3 ghante dhoop mein chhodo. Check karne se pehle guess karo thaili ke andar kya dikhega.
items.answer: Water droplets on the inside of the bag, because leaves lose water vapour through stomata (transpiration), which condenses on the bag.
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason first
Point to what leaves might give off
Prompt: leaves lose water ___ through stomata
Assert: droplets form from transpired water vapour

verified.solverAnswer: Water droplets/mist on inside of the bag from water vapour lost by leaves (transpiration).

items.prompt_en: A leaf is placed in a sealed jar in bright sunlight, and another in a sealed jar in the dark, for several hours. Predict in which jar the oxygen level goes up and in which it goes down.
items.prompt_hi: Ek patta band jaar mein tez dhoop mein, aur doosra band jaar mein andhere mein, kuch ghante rakha. Guess karo kis jaar mein oxygen badhegi aur kis mein ghategi.
items.answer: Oxygen goes up in the jar in sunlight (photosynthesis is faster than respiration) and goes down in the dark jar (only respiration uses oxygen).
acceptable: up in light, down in dark
dhoop mein badhegi, andhere mein ghategi
hints: Ask for a guess before reveal
Point to which process needs light
Prompt: in the dark only ___ happens
Assert: light jar gains oxygen; dark jar loses oxygen

verified.solverAnswer: Light jar: oxygen goes up (photosynthesis exceeds respiration); dark jar: oxygen goes down (only respiration).

items.prompt_en: What are stomata, and where are most of them found on a leaf?
items.prompt_hi: Stomata kya hote hain, aur patte pe zyada-tar kahaan milte hain?
items.answer: Tiny pores in the leaf surface, each controlled by two guard cells; most are on the lower surface of leaves.
acceptable: tiny pores on the lower surface
hints: Ask what the word 'pore' means
Think about which side faces away from the direct sun
Prompt: mostly on the ___ surface
Assert: tiny pores, mostly on the underside

verified.solverAnswer: Tiny pores on leaves for gas exchange and water loss; mostly on the lower (under) surface.

items.prompt_en: What do guard cells do?
items.prompt_hi: Guard cells kya kaam karte hain?
items.answer: They open and close each stoma, controlling how much gas enters and leaves and how much water vapour is lost.
hints: Ask what 'guard' suggests
Point to the two cells around each pore
Prompt: they ___ and ___ the pore
Assert: they open and close stomata

verified.solverAnswer: Two guard cells open and close the stoma (pore).

items.prompt_en: Why are most stomata on the lower surface of a leaf rather than the upper surface?
items.prompt_hi: Zyada-tar stomata patte ki neeche wali satah pe kyun hote hain, upar wali pe kyun nahi?
items.answer: The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water is lost through the stomata there, while gases can still be exchanged.
hints: Ask which side gets the direct sun
Point to heat making water evaporate faster
Prompt: the lower side loses ___ water
Assert: less water is lost from the shaded underside

verified.solverAnswer: Lower side is shaded and cooler, less sun, so less water lost by evaporation; still exchange gases.

items.prompt_en: Compare the gas exchange of a leaf at 12 noon on a sunny day and at midnight.
items.prompt_hi: Dhoop wale din dopahar 12 baje aur aadhi raat ko patte ki gas exchange ki tulna karo.
items.answer: Noon: photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so net carbon dioxide goes in and oxygen comes out. Midnight: only respiration, so oxygen goes in and carbon dioxide comes out.
acceptable: noon CO2 in O2 out; midnight O2 in CO2 out
hints: Ask which processes happen at noon
And at midnight?
Prompt: at night the leaf takes in ___
Assert: noon net O2 out; midnight O2 in

verified.solverAnswer: Noon: photosynthesis fast, takes in CO2 and gives out O2 (net), plus respiration and transpiration. Midnight: no photosynthesis; respiration only, takes in O2, gives out CO2.

items.prompt_en: Meena writes: 'At night plants stop all activity and no gases pass through the stomata.' Correct her.
items.prompt_hi: Meena likhti hai: 'Raat ko paudhe sab kaam band kar dete hain aur stomata se koi gas nahi jaati.' Use sahi karo.
items.answer: Plants keep respiring at night, so oxygen still enters and carbon dioxide leaves; only photosynthesis stops without light.
hints: Ask whether plant cells need energy at night
Which process stops without light?
Prompt: only ___ stops
Assert: respiration continues; only photosynthesis stops

verified.solverAnswer: Plants respire at night; stomata still allow oxygen in and CO2 out; only photosynthesis stops.

items.prompt_en: Describe what you would see under a microscope in a thin peel from the lower side of a leaf, and draw (or describe) one stoma with its guard cells.
items.prompt_hi: Patte ki neeche wali satah ki patli jhilli microscope mein dekhne pe kya dikhega, batao, aur ek stoma ko guard cells ke saath banao (ya batao).
items.answer: Many cells fitting together like tiles, with small openings scattered among them; each stoma looks like a slit between two bean- or kidney-shaped guard cells.
acceptable: slit between two bean-shaped guard cells
hints: Ask what shape guard cells are
Point to the gap between them
Prompt: a slit between two ___-shaped cells
Assert: a pore between two bean-shaped guard cells

verified.solverAnswer: A thin transparent layer with pairs of bean-shaped guard cells enclosing a tiny gap (stoma) amid irregular epidermal cells; guard cells have chloroplasts.

items.prompt_en: Gardeners spray water on leaves in hot summer evenings, and many desert plants have very few stomata or tiny leaves. Explain the link.
items.prompt_hi: Maali garmi ki shaam ko patton pe paani chhidakte hain, aur registaan ke paudhon mein stomata bahut kam ya patte chhote hote hain. Inmein connection samjhao.
items.answer: Both reduce water loss: in heat, transpiration through stomata is high; desert plants save water by having fewer stomata or tiny leaves (or spines), giving less surface for water to escape.
hints: Ask what heat does to water loss
Point to cactus spines being reduced leaves
Prompt: fewer stomata means less ___
Assert: less surface and fewer stomata save water

verified.solverAnswer: Desert plants reduce water loss through few stomata/small or spiny leaves; gardeners spraying cools leaves and reduces transpiration stress.

items.prompt_en: City planners plant rows of trees along hot roads, and say this cools the area. Use transpiration to explain how.
items.prompt_hi: Shehar ke planners garam sadkon ke kinaare pedon ki kataar lagaate hain aur kehte hain isse ilaaka thanda hota hai. Transpiration se samjhao kaise.
items.answer: Trees give off large amounts of water vapour through their stomata; evaporation of this water takes heat from the leaves and surroundings, cooling the air, and the trees also give shade.
acceptable: evaporation of transpired water cools the air, plus shade
hints: Ask what happens to your skin when sweat evaporates
Point to trees losing water vapour
Prompt: evaporating water takes away ___
Assert: transpiration cools the air; shade helps too

verified.solverAnswer: Trees release water vapour through transpiration; evaporation takes heat from surroundings, cooling the air; also shade.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your friend what stomata are and the three things that pass through them.
items.prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao stomata kya hain aur unse kaunsi teen cheezein aati-jaati hain.
items.answer: Key ideas: tiny pores, mostly on the underside of leaves, opened and closed by guard cells; carbon dioxide and oxygen pass through for photosynthesis and respiration; water vapour escapes in transpiration.
acceptable: pores, guard cells, CO2, O2, water vapour
hints: Ask where stomata are and what controls them
Name the gases first
Prompt: and also water ___
Assert: CO2, O2 and water vapour pass through

verified.solverAnswer: Stomata are tiny pores in leaves; carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour pass through.

items.prompt_en: From memory: what is the loss of water vapour from leaves called?
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: patton se paani ki bhaap ka nikalna kya kehlaata hai?
items.answer: Transpiration.
hints: It is like a plant's sweating
Starts with 'trans'
Prompt: ___
Assert: transpiration

verified.solverAnswer: Transpiration.

workedExample.problem: What gases does a neem leaf exchange during one full day?
steps: Morning to evening (light): photosynthesis and respiration both happen
Photosynthesis is faster in good light, so the leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen overall
At night (dark): photosynthesis stops; respiration continues
So at night the leaf takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide
Throughout, water vapour escapes through the stomata (transpiration), less when stomata close in heat or darkness
fadedVersion: In light: photosynthesis and ___ both happen
Photosynthesis is faster, so overall carbon dioxide goes ___ and oxygen goes ___
At night: ___ stops; respiration continues
So at night the leaf takes in ___
Water vapour escapes by ___

skills.title: Explain that roots absorb water and minerals, which travel up through xylem to all parts
Explain that food made in leaves travels through phloem to all parts, including roots and fruits
Link transpiration to the upward pull of water

expectations: Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil, mainly through tiny root hairs.
Xylem is a system of tube-like vessels that carries water and minerals upward from the roots, through the stem, to the leaves and other parts.
Phloem carries food (sugars) made in the leaves to all parts of the plant: up to growing buds and fruits and down to roots and storage organs.
Water evaporating from leaves through stomata (transpiration) creates a pull that helps draw water up through the xylem, even in very tall trees.

misconceptions.belief: Water moves down from leaves to roots.
signs: Says rain falls on leaves and 'goes down to the roots'
Thinks watering leaves is the main way to water a plant

diagnostic.prompt_en: A white flower's stalk is placed in water coloured with food colour. After some hours the petals show the colour. In which direction did the water move?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Safed phool ki daandi ko food colour wale paani mein rakha. Kuch ghanton baad pankhudiyon mein rang aa gaya. Paani kis disha mein chala?

options.text: Up the stem from the water to the petals
Down from the petals to the water
The colour just floated in through the air

remediation.representation: Time-lapse of a white carnation or chrysanthemum turning blue from the bottom up
remediation.moveShape: Ask where the colour appeared first and last, and what that says about direction

misconceptions.belief: Food made in the leaves stays in the leaves, or only moves upward like water.
signs: Cannot explain how potatoes or carrots store food underground
Thinks roots make their own food

diagnostic.prompt_en: Carrots and potatoes store a lot of food underground. Where was that food made, and how did it get there?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Gaajar aur aaloo zameen ke neeche bahut khaana jama karte hain. Woh khaana kahaan bana tha aur wahaan kaise pahuncha?

options.text: Made in the root itself from soil
Made in the leaves and carried down through phloem
Made in the leaves and carried down through xylem

remediation.representation: Two-colour tube diagram: blue xylem arrows going up, orange phloem arrows going both up and down
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to place arrows from the leaf to a potato and to a mango

items.prompt_en: Put a white flower (or a stalk of celery) in a glass of water with a few drops of food colour. Before waiting, predict what you will see after a few hours, and where the colour will appear first.
items.prompt_hi: Ek safed phool (ya celery ki daandi) ko kuch boond food colour wale paani ke glass mein rakho. Intezaar se pehle guess karo kuch ghanton mein kya dikhega, aur rang sabse pehle kahaan aayega.
items.answer: The colour rises up the stem and appears in the petals (or leaf veins), first near the bottom and then at the top, because water travels up through the xylem.
acceptable: colour goes up to the petals
hints: Ask for a guess and a reason
Point to the stem as a pipe
Prompt: water moves ___ the stem
Assert: colour rises up through the xylem into the petals

verified.solverAnswer: Colour travels up the stem and appears in petals/leaf veins first at the tips; water rises through xylem.

items.prompt_en: Two identical leafy twigs are placed in equal measuring cylinders of water, with a drop of oil on top to stop evaporation from the surface. One twig has its leaves removed. Predict which cylinder loses more water in a day, and why.
items.prompt_hi: Do ek jaisi patteedaar tehniyaan barabar paani wale cylinders mein rakhi hain, upar tel ki boond hai taaki satah se paani na udey. Ek tehni ke patte hata diye. Guess karo ek din mein kis cylinder ka paani zyada kam hoga, aur kyun.
items.answer: The cylinder with the leafy twig loses more water, because leaves transpire through stomata, which pulls water up the stem.
hints: Ask for a guess first
Point to where water escapes from a plant
Prompt: leaves lose water by ___
Assert: the leafy twig, because transpiration pulls water up

verified.solverAnswer: The leafy twig loses more water because leaves transpire and pull water up; the leafless one loses little.

items.prompt_en: Which tissue carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves?
items.prompt_hi: Kaunsa tissue paani aur minerals ko jadon se patton tak le jaata hai?
items.answer: Xylem.
hints: Two tissue names: xylem and phloem
This one carries water
Prompt: x___
Assert: xylem

verified.solverAnswer: Xylem.

items.prompt_en: Which tissue carries food from the leaves to other parts?
items.prompt_hi: Kaunsa tissue patton se khaana baaki hisson tak le jaata hai?
items.answer: Phloem.
hints: Two tissue names again
This one carries food
Prompt: ph___
Assert: phloem

verified.solverAnswer: Phloem.

items.prompt_en: Why do we water the soil around a plant rather than just spraying its leaves?
items.prompt_hi: Hum paudhe ke patton pe hi paani chhidakne ki jagah jad ke paas mitti mein paani kyun daalte hain?
items.answer: Because water is absorbed by the roots from the soil and carried up through the xylem; leaves do not absorb most of the water a plant needs.
hints: Ask which part drinks the water
Point to root hairs
Prompt: water enters through the ___
Assert: roots absorb water, which travels up the xylem

verified.solverAnswer: Roots (root hairs) absorb water from soil; leaves absorb very little; water is carried up through xylem.

items.prompt_en: Compare xylem and phloem: what each carries and in which direction.
items.prompt_hi: Xylem aur phloem ki tulna karo: dono kya le jaate hain aur kis disha mein.
items.answer: Xylem carries water and minerals upward from roots; phloem carries food from leaves to all parts, both upward and downward.
acceptable: xylem water up; phloem food both ways
hints: Ask which one starts at the roots
Which one starts at the leaves?
Prompt: phloem goes up ___ down
Assert: xylem water up; phloem food in all directions

verified.solverAnswer: Xylem carries water and minerals upward only from roots to leaves; phloem carries food (sugar) from leaves to all parts, up or down.

items.prompt_en: Aman says: 'A potato makes its own food under the ground from the soil.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Aman kehta hai: 'Aaloo zameen ke neeche mitti se apna khaana khud banaata hai.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: A potato cannot photosynthesise underground in the dark; food is made in the leaves and carried down through the phloem to be stored in the potato as starch.
acceptable: made in leaves, carried by phloem
hints: Ask whether there is sunlight underground
Where is food made?
Prompt: food comes down through the ___
Assert: food made in leaves is carried down by phloem

verified.solverAnswer: Potato can't make food underground (no light, no chlorophyll); food is made in leaves and carried down by phloem and stored in potato tuber.

items.prompt_en: Draw a plant with two colours of arrows (or describe them): one for water and minerals, one for food. Show where each starts and ends.
items.prompt_hi: Do rang ke teer wala paudha banao (ya batao): ek paani aur minerals ke liye, ek khaane ke liye. Dikhaao har ek kahaan se shuru aur kahaan khatam hota hai.
items.answer: Water arrows: from roots up the stem to the leaves (xylem). Food arrows: from leaves to buds, flowers, fruits upward and to roots or tubers downward (phloem).
acceptable: water arrows up from roots; food arrows from leaves both ways
hints: Ask where water starts
Where does food start?
Prompt: food arrows point ___ and ___
Assert: water up from roots; food out from leaves in both directions

verified.solverAnswer: Blue arrows (water/minerals): from root hairs up the stem to leaves. Red arrows (food): from leaves to all parts, down to roots, fruits and tuber.

items.prompt_en: A potted plant's leaves droop on a hot afternoon even though the soil is a little moist. Explain using transpiration and water transport.
items.prompt_hi: Garam dopahar mein gamle ke paudhe ke patte murjha jaate hain jabki mitti thodi geeli hai. Transpiration aur paani ke transport se samjhao.
items.answer: In heat, leaves lose water by transpiration faster than roots can absorb and xylem can supply it, so cells lose water and the leaves droop; they usually recover in the evening.
acceptable: losing water faster than it is supplied
hints: Ask what heat does to water loss from leaves
Compare loss with supply
Prompt: loss is ___ than supply
Assert: transpiration faster than water supply makes leaves droop

verified.solverAnswer: Transpiration on a hot afternoon is faster than water supply, so leaves lose turgor and droop; recovers in evening.

items.prompt_en: A giant banyan or a tall coconut tree has no pump, yet water reaches leaves many metres up. Explain how.
items.prompt_hi: Bade bargad ya oonche naariyal ke ped mein koi pump nahi hota, phir bhi paani kai meter upar patton tak pahunch jaata hai. Samjhao kaise.
items.answer: Water evaporates from the leaves through stomata (transpiration), and this creates a pull that draws a continuous column of water up through the narrow xylem tubes from the roots.
hints: Ask what happens at the top when water leaves the leaves
Think of sucking through a straw
Prompt: transpiration creates a ___
Assert: transpiration pull draws water up the xylem

verified.solverAnswer: Transpiration from leaves creates suction (transpiration pull), water molecules stick together and column of water is pulled up xylem; root pressure helps.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger child how the water you pour on a tulsi plant reaches its top leaves, and how the food made in the leaves reaches its roots.
items.prompt_hi: Chhote bachche ko samjhao ki tulsi pe daala hua paani upar ke patton tak kaise pahunchta hai, aur patton mein bana khaana jadon tak kaise.
items.answer: Key ideas: roots absorb water and minerals; xylem carries them up; transpiration from leaves helps pull water up; leaves make food; phloem carries food to all parts, including the roots.
acceptable: roots, xylem up, transpiration pull, phloem to all parts
hints: Ask which part drinks first
Which tubes carry water up?
Prompt: food goes down through the ___
Assert: xylem carries water up; phloem carries food everywhere

verified.solverAnswer: Roots drink water; it goes up through thin tubes (xylem) to leaves; leaves make food that travels through phloem down to roots and everywhere.

items.prompt_en: From memory: what are the tiny hair-like outgrowths on roots that absorb water called?
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: jadon ke woh chhote baal jaise ubhaar jo paani sokhte hain, kya kehlaate hain?
items.answer: Root hairs.
hints: They are near the tip of the root
They look like tiny hairs
Prompt: root ___
Assert: root hairs

verified.solverAnswer: Root hairs.
verified.note: HINT LEAK (mild): hints 1-2 ('near the tip of the root', 'look like tiny hairs') nearly spell out 'root hairs'.

workedExample.problem: How does water from the soil reach the leaves of a tomato plant?
steps: Absorb: root hairs take in water and dissolved minerals from the soil
Enter: the water passes into the xylem in the root
Rise: xylem tubes carry water up the stem to the leaves
Pull: water evaporating from leaves through stomata (transpiration) pulls more water up
Use: leaves use some water for photosynthesis; the food made goes out through the phloem
fadedVersion: Absorb: ___ take in water from the soil
Enter: water passes into the ___
Rise: tubes carry water ___ the stem
Pull: ___ from the leaves pulls more water up
Use: food made in leaves leaves through the ___

skills.title: Classify objects as luminous (give out their own light) or non-luminous (seen by light they reflect)
Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque by how much light passes through
Explain that we see non-luminous objects because light from a source bounces off them into our eyes

expectations: Luminous objects give out their own light: the Sun, other stars, a candle flame, a glowing bulb, a firefly.

Non-luminous objects do not give out their own light; we see them only when light from a source falls on them and is reflected into our eyes. The Moon is non-luminous: it shines by reflecting sunlight.
Transparent materials let almost all light pass so we can see clearly through them (clear glass, clean water, air).
Translucent materials let some light pass but we cannot see clearly through them (butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper).
Opaque materials do not let light pass (cardboard, wood, a steel plate, a brick wall).

misconceptions.belief: The Moon is a source of light because it shines brightly at night.
signs: Lists the Moon with the Sun as luminous
Says the Moon makes its own light
Cannot explain the Moon's phases or why it is dark during a lunar eclipse

diagnostic.prompt_en: On a full moon night the Moon looks very bright. Where does its light come from?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Poornima ki raat chaand bahut chamakdaar dikhta hai. Uski roshni kahaan se aati hai?

options.text: The Moon makes its own light, like a lamp
Sunlight falls on the Moon and is reflected towards Earth
The stars light it up

remediation.representation: A torch (Sun), a steel bowl (Moon) and the child's eye in a dark room: the bowl shines only when the torch is on
remediation.moveShape: Switch the torch off and ask why the 'moon' disappeared

misconceptions.belief: We see things because light comes out of our eyes, or we can see objects even in total darkness if we look hard.
signs: Says 'my eyes send out light to see'
Thinks eyes adjust to complete darkness given time

diagnostic.prompt_en: In a room with no windows and the light off (completely dark), can you see a red ball on the table?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Bina khidki wale kamre mein, light band (bilkul andhera), kya tum mez pe rakhi laal ball dekh sakte ho?

options.text: Yes, if you look carefully for a long time
No, because no light falls on the ball to be reflected into your eyes
Yes, because the ball is red and bright

remediation.representation: Arrow diagram: source to object to eye, with the arrow from source removed in darkness
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to trace the light path for seeing a book, then remove the source

misconceptions.belief: Translucent and transparent mean the same thing; any material that lets some light through is transparent.
signs: Calls butter paper transparent
Mixes up 'can see light' and 'can see clearly through'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Holding butter paper in front of a torch, you can see a glow but not the torch clearly. What is butter paper?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Torch ke saamne butter paper rakhne pe roshni ki chamak dikhti hai par torch saaf nahi dikhti. Butter paper kya hai?

options.text: Transparent
Translucent
Opaque

remediation.representation: Three-window card: clear glass (see clearly), butter paper (glow only), cardboard (nothing)
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to hold each in front of a torch and describe what they see

items.prompt_en: Sort into luminous and non-luminous: Sun, Moon, candle flame, mirror, firefly, notebook.
items.prompt_hi: Luminous aur non-luminous mein baanto: Sooraj, Chaand, mombatti ki lau, sheesha, jugnu, copy.
items.answer: Luminous: Sun, candle flame, firefly. Non-luminous: Moon, mirror, notebook.
acceptable: luminous Sun flame firefly; non-luminous Moon mirror notebook
hints: Ask which ones would glow in a dark room on their own
Point to the Moon needing the Sun
Prompt: the Moon is ___
Assert: Sun, flame, firefly luminous; Moon, mirror, notebook non-luminous

verified.solverAnswer: Luminous: Sun, candle flame, firefly. Non-luminous: Moon, mirror, notebook.

items.prompt_en: Hold a clear glass sheet, a sheet of butter paper and a piece of cardboard in front of a lit torch one by one. Before you try, predict what you will see through each.
items.prompt_hi: Ek-ek karke saaf kaanch, butter paper aur gatte ko jalti torch ke saamne rakho. Karne se pehle guess karo har ek se kya dikhega.
items.answer: Glass: the torch is seen clearly (transparent). Butter paper: only a glow, not clearly (translucent). Cardboard: no light (opaque).
hints: Ask for a guess for each
Point to how much light each might let through
Prompt: glass clear, butter paper ___, cardboard ___
Assert: transparent, translucent, opaque

verified.solverAnswer: Glass: clear view (transparent); butter paper: blurry glow (translucent); cardboard: nothing (opaque).

items.prompt_en: In a dark room, shine a torch onto a steel bowl so that it 'shines'. Predict what happens to the bowl's brightness when you switch the torch off, and what this tells you about the Moon.
items.prompt_hi: Andhere kamre mein torch steel ki katori pe daalo taaki woh chamke. Guess karo torch band karne pe katori ki chamak ka kya hoga, aur isse Chaand ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai.
items.answer: The bowl goes dark immediately, because it was only reflecting the torch's light; the Moon similarly shines only by reflecting sunlight.
hints: Ask for a guess first
Point to whether the bowl makes its own light
Prompt: the bowl only ___ light
Assert: it goes dark; the Moon shines by reflected sunlight

verified.solverAnswer: It goes dark; bowl only reflects light; Moon shines by reflected sunlight.

items.prompt_en: Why can you see this page, even though the page does not give out light?
items.prompt_hi: Ye page khud roshni nahi deta, phir bhi tum ise kaise dekh paate ho?
items.answer: Light from a source (a bulb or the Sun) falls on the page and is reflected into our eyes.
hints: Ask where the light in the room comes from
Trace it to the page and then to you
Prompt: light bounces off the page into our ___
Assert: reflected light from a source enters our eyes

verified.solverAnswer: Light from a source falls on the page, is reflected and enters your eyes.

items.prompt_en: Frosted glass is used in bathroom windows and clear glass in shop windows. Explain why using the words transparent and translucent.
items.prompt_hi: Bathroom ki khidki mein frosted glass aur dukaan ki khidki mein saaf glass lagaate hain. Transparent aur translucent shabdon se samjhao kyun.
items.answer: Frosted glass is translucent: it lets light in but people cannot see clearly through it, giving privacy; clear shop glass is transparent so customers can see the goods.
acceptable: frosted translucent for privacy; clear transparent to see goods
hints: Ask what a bathroom needs that a shop does not
Point to light passing vs seeing clearly
Prompt: frosted glass is ___
Assert: translucent for privacy; transparent to display

verified.solverAnswer: Frosted glass is translucent: lets light in but gives privacy; clear glass is transparent so one can see goods through it.

items.prompt_en: Pooja says: 'The Moon is luminous because it is the brightest thing in the night sky.' Correct her.
items.prompt_hi: Pooja kehti hai: 'Chaand luminous hai kyunki raat ke aasmaan mein sabse chamakdaar hai.' Use sahi karo.
items.answer: Brightness does not make something luminous; the Moon does not make its own light, it reflects sunlight, so it is non-luminous.
hints: Ask whether being bright means making light
What does the Moon reflect?
Prompt: the Moon ___ sunlight
Assert: the Moon is non-luminous; it reflects sunlight

verified.solverAnswer: The Moon is non-luminous; it reflects sunlight; brightness doesn't mean it makes light.

items.prompt_en: Classify: a clean plastic water bottle, a sheet of oiled paper, a wooden door, still pond water, a steel tiffin box.
items.prompt_hi: Classify karo: saaf plastic ki paani ki bottle, tel laga kaagaz, lakdi ka darwaaza, shaant taalaab ka saaf paani, steel ka tiffin.
items.answer: Transparent: clean plastic bottle, clean pond water (if clear). Translucent: oiled paper. Opaque: wooden door, steel tiffin.
acceptable: bottle and clear water transparent; oiled paper translucent; door and tiffin opaque
hints: Ask which ones you can see through clearly
Which let only some light through?
Prompt: oiled paper is ___
Assert: two transparent, one translucent, two opaque

verified.solverAnswer: Plastic bottle: transparent; oiled paper: translucent; wooden door: opaque; clear pond water: transparent; steel tiffin: opaque.

items.prompt_en: Draw (or describe) arrows showing how you see a mango on the table in a room lit by a bulb.
items.prompt_hi: Bulb se roshan kamre mein mez pe rakha aam tum kaise dekhte ho, teer se dikhaao (ya batao).
items.answer: An arrow from the bulb to the mango, then an arrow from the mango to the eye: light from the bulb falls on the mango and is reflected into the eye.
hints: Ask where the light starts
Where does it go next?
Prompt: bulb to ___ to ___
Assert: source to object to eye

verified.solverAnswer: Arrows: bulb to mango (light travels from bulb), mango to eye (reflected light enters eye).

items.prompt_en: Fireflies glow on summer nights in villages, and some deep-sea fish glow too. Are they luminous or non-luminous? Why might glowing be useful to them?
items.prompt_hi: Garmi ki raaton mein gaon mein jugnu chamakte hain, aur kuch gehre samundar ki machhliyan bhi chamakti hain. Ye luminous hain ya non-luminous? Chamakna unke liye kyun useful ho sakta hai?
items.answer: Luminous, because they make their own light. Glowing can help them find mates, attract prey or communicate in the dark.
acceptable: luminous; to attract mates or prey
hints: Ask whether they need another light to glow
Think of what happens in total darkness
Prompt: they make their ___ light
Assert: luminous; useful for signalling and attracting

verified.solverAnswer: Luminous (make their own light, bioluminescence); useful to signal mates, attract prey, confuse predators.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque, with one example from your house for each.
items.prompt_hi: Dost ko transparent, translucent aur opaque ka farak samjhao, ghar se har ek ka ek example dekar.
items.answer: Key ideas: transparent lets almost all light pass so we see clearly (window glass); translucent lets some light pass but not clearly (butter paper, frosted glass); opaque lets no light pass (door, wall).
hints: Start with how much light passes
Give an example of each
Prompt: opaque lets ___ light through
Assert: all, some, none, with examples

verified.solverAnswer: Transparent: lets almost all light through, can see clearly (window glass). Translucent: lets some light, blurry (butter paper, frosted glass). Opaque: lets none (wooden door).

items.prompt_en: From memory: give two examples of luminous objects.
items.prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: do luminous cheezon ke naam.
items.answer: Any two: Sun, stars, candle flame, lit bulb, firefly, glowing torch.
hints: Think of things that glow by themselves
One is up in the sky in the day
Prompt: the ___ and a ___
Assert: e.g., Sun and a candle flame

verified.solverAnswer: Sun and a candle flame (also firefly, bulb).

workedExample.problem: Is a lit bulb, a steel plate and a sheet of tracing paper luminous or non-luminous, and how much light passes through each?
